characters.name: Sherlock Holmes
characters.description: A character with a cold, precise, and admirably balanced mind, who is described as the most perfect reasoning and observing machine. He loathed every form of society and had a singular regard for Irene Adler. | Investigating the King's case. | My companion, who staggers back white with chagrin and surprise upon hearing Irene Adler has left. | A consulting detective known for his deductive reasoning. | A consulting detective known for his keen powers of observation and deduction. | A consulting detective with extraordinary powers of observation and deduction, currently engrossed in a new problem. | A consulting detective, known for his keen observational and deductive skills. | A keen reasoner who changes his costume and manner to suit his investigations. | Consulting detective listening to the King's problem. | Consulting detective, currently discussing a case with Watson. | Discusses the case with the King and Watson, receives payment and Mademoiselle's address, and plans the next steps. | Emerged from his bedroom tweed-suited and respectable, laughed heartily, and recounted his morning's activities. | Involved in a street scuffle, protecting a lady, and gets injured. | Loathed society, alternated between cocaine and ambition, deeply attracted by the study of crime, possessed immense faculties and extraordinary powers of observation. | Participating in a staged event to retrieve a photograph. | Returns to Baker Street disguised as a drunken groom, then changes into his usual tweed suit. | The detective, depicted as languid but highly perceptive. | The detective, who explains a plan and disguises himself as a Nonconformist clergyman. | The famous consulting detective, addressed by the client. | Recipient of Irene Adler's letter. | Referred to by Irene Adler in her letter. | The detective who investigated the case, receiving the letter from Irene Norton and later requesting her photograph as a reward. | The detective whose plans were thwarted by Irene Adler's wit.

characters.name: Irene Adler
characters.description: A well-known adventuress, born in New Jersey in 1858, who was a contralto and prima donna at La Scala and the Imperial Opera of Warsaw, now retired and living in London. | A woman whose photograph is central to the scandal, known for her wit. | Referred to by Sherlock Holmes as 'the woman', she eclipses and predominates the whole of her sex in his eyes. She is described as 'the late Irene Adler, of dubious and questionable memory'. | The bride in an impromptu wedding, who gives the narrator a sovereign. | The daintiest thing under a bonnet on this planet; lives quietly, sings at concerts, drives out at five every day, and returns at seven sharp for dinner; seldom goes out at other times, except when she sings. | The lady Holmes was protecting, who directs him to be brought into Briony Lodge after his injury. | The lady who has left England with her husband for the Continent. | Woman involved in the King's scandal, now married. | Woman who outwitted Sherlock Holmes, now married and fleeing. | Woman who possesses a compromising photograph of herself and the King, threatening to use it. | The subject of Holmes's morning investigation. | The woman Holmes plans to meet at Briony Lodge.

characters.name: Atkinson brothers
characters.description: Victims of a singular tragedy that Holmes cleared up.

characters.name: Watson
characters.description: A doctor and Holmes's companion, who has recently gained weight and returned to medical practice. | Holmes's companion and chronicler, present during the discussion and client's arrival. | Present during Holmes's discussion with the King, and later returns to Baker Street as requested by Holmes. | The narrator, addressed by Holmes. | Holmes's friend and colleague, present during the client's arrival. | Holmes's friend and colleague, who occasionally assists him in his cases.

characters.name: Mary Jane
characters.description: Watson's servant girl, described as incorrigible and careless.

characters.name: Count Von Kramm
characters.description: A mysterious visitor with a marked German accent, claiming to be a Bohemian nobleman, but later admitting his title is an alias. He is an agent for an 'august person'.

characters.name: Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein, Grand Duke of Cassel-Felstein, and hereditary King of Bohemia
characters.occupation: hereditary King of Bohemia, Grand Duke of Cassel-Felstein
characters.description: The client, initially disguised, who reveals his true royal identity.

characters.name: Clotilde Lothman von Saxe-Meningen
characters.description: Second daughter of the King of Scandinavia, to whom the King is about to be married.

characters.name: Godfrey Norton
characters.description: A character who urgently calls upon Holmes inside the Church of St. Monica. | The groom in an impromptu wedding, who drags the narrator to be a witness. | A person whose knowledge of the photograph complicates matters. | Dark, handsome, and dashing; never calls less than once a day, and often twice; of the Inner Temple. | Irene Adler's husband.

characters.name: Mrs. Turner
characters.description: The landlady who provides food for Holmes and the Doctor.

characters.name: Mr. John Hare
characters.description: An actor whose ability to change character is compared to Holmes's. | Irene Adler's coachman, sent to watch Holmes.

characters.name: King of Bohemia
characters.description: A royal figure who is capable of having someone waylaid and searched. | The King of Bohemia, who is amazed by Holmes's request for Irene's photograph. | The client who employed an agent (Holmes) and is wronged by Irene Adler. | The client, referred to as 'the King' and 'his Majesty'. | The monarch who is attempting to retrieve a compromising photograph from a woman. | Client of Sherlock Holmes, concerned about a potential scandal. | The client who sought Holmes's help, relieved by Irene's letter and offering Holmes a reward.

characters.name: IRENE NORTON, _née_ ADLER
characters.description: The woman who wrote the letter resolving the potential scandal, stating she loves another man and will not use the photograph against the King.

crimes.name: Potential Scandal of the House of Ormstein
crimes.description: A delicate matter that could grow into an immense scandal, seriously compromising one of the reigning families of Europe, specifically the great House of Ormstein, hereditary kings of Bohemia. | A delicate matter that could seriously compromise one of the reigning families of Europe, specifically the great House of Ormstein. | A great scandal that threatened to affect the kingdom of Bohemia. | Irene Adler threatens to send a compromising photograph of herself and the King to the family of his fiancée, Clotilde Lothman von Saxe-Meningen, to prevent his marriage. | The King of Bohemia seeks to retrieve compromising letters from Irene Adler to prevent her from using them for blackmail or other purposes that would cause a scandal for his house. | The King seeks to prevent the public release of a compromising photograph that could lead to a scandal and jeopardize his betrothal. | The King's fear of annoyance due to Irene Adler possessing a compromising photograph that could ruin his marriage. | The current inquiry Holmes is working on, involving a client of exalted station. | The ongoing threat involving a photograph that could cause a scandal for the House of Ormstein. | The overarching mystery Holmes is investigating, concerning a compromising photograph and its potential to cause a scandal for the King of Bohemia. | The overarching scandal Holmes is investigating, involving a photograph that could lead to a royal marriage being jeopardized. | The potential exposure of a compromising photograph involving the King of Bohemia. | The potential scandal involving a photograph that could compromise the House of Ormstein. | The potential scandal involving a photograph that could compromise the King of Bohemia, now resolved by Irene Norton's letter. | The potential scandal involving the King of Bohemia and Irene Adler, which is the reason for Holmes's investigation. | The underlying mystery Holmes is trying to solve, involving a compromising photograph.
crimes.motive: To prevent a scandal that could impact European history and compromise a royal family.

deductions.observation: Holmes observes Watson's overall healthy and content appearance.
deductions.inference: Such an appearance is consistent with a happy marriage.
deductions.conclusion: Wedlock suits Watson.

deductions.observation: Holmes visually assesses Watson's physical build.
deductions.inference: Watson's current physique indicates an increase in weight.
deductions.conclusion: Watson has put on seven and a half pounds.

deductions.observation: Holmes observes subtle cues about Watson's current habits or appearance.
deductions.inference: These cues suggest Watson has resumed his medical profession.
deductions.conclusion: Watson is in practice again.

deductions.observation: Holmes observes physical evidence on Watson (e.g., condition of clothes, shoes, or general dampness).
deductions.inference: This evidence indicates recent exposure to rain or water.
deductions.conclusion: Watson has been getting very wet lately.

deductions.observation: Holmes observes some detail on Watson's clothing or person (e.g., a stain, a tear, or a general lack of meticulous care).
deductions.inference: This detail suggests that the person responsible for Watson's personal care (a servant) is clumsy and careless.
deductions.conclusion: Watson has a most clumsy and careless servant girl.

deductions.observation: on the inside of your left shoe, just where the firelight strikes it, the leather is scored by six almost parallel cuts.
deductions.inference: they have been caused by someone who has very carelessly scraped round the edges of the sole in order to remove crusted mud from it.
deductions.conclusion: you had been out in vile weather, and that you had a particularly malignant boot-slitting specimen of the London slavey.

deductions.observation: a gentleman walks into my rooms smelling of iodoform, with a black mark of nitrate of silver upon his right forefinger, and a bulge on the right side of his top-hat to show where he has secreted his stethoscope
deductions.conclusion: an active member of the medical profession.

deductions.observation: The narrator has frequently seen the steps leading from the hall to this room but cannot state their number.
deductions.conclusion: You see, but you do not observe. The distinction is clear.

deductions.observation: Holmes has both seen and observed the steps leading from the hall to his room.
deductions.conclusion: I know that there are seventeen steps.

deductions.observation: The paper upon which the note was written.
deductions.inference: Such paper could not be bought under half a crown a packet. It is peculiarly strong and stiff.
deductions.conclusion: The man who wrote it was presumably well to do.

deductions.observation: The peculiar quality of the paper.
deductions.inference: It is not an English paper at all.
deductions.conclusion: The paper is of foreign origin.

deductions.observation: A large 'E' with a small 'g,' a 'P,' and a large 'G' with a small 't' woven into the texture of the paper.
deductions.inference: The 'G' with the small 't' stands for 'Gesellschaft' (German for 'Company'), and 'P' stands for 'Papier'.
deductions.conclusion: The watermark indicates a German paper manufacturer.

deductions.observation: The 'Eg' from the watermark, combined with the German origin.
deductions.inference: Consulting the Continental Gazetteer for place names starting with 'Eg' in German-speaking regions.
deductions.conclusion: The paper comes from Egria, a city in Bohemia, known for its paper-mills.

deductions.observation: The paper was made in Bohemia.
deductions.inference: The writer used paper from Bohemia.
deductions.conclusion: The paper was made in Bohemia.

deductions.observation: The peculiar construction of the sentence—'This account of you we have from all quarters received.'
deductions.inference: A Frenchman or Russian could not have written that. It is the German who is so uncourteous to his verbs.
deductions.conclusion: The man who wrote the note is a German.

deductions.observation: Sharp sound of horses' hoofs and grating wheels against the curb, followed by a sharp pull at the bell.
deductions.inference: A pair, by the sound.
deductions.conclusion: The arriving party is using a carriage drawn by a pair of horses.

deductions.observation: A nice little brougham and a pair of beauties (horses).
deductions.inference: A hundred and fifty guineas apiece (estimation of the horses' value).
deductions.conclusion: There's money in this case, Watson, if there is nothing else (the client is wealthy).

deductions.observation: The visitor, who introduced himself as Count Von Kramm, states that 'the title by which I have just called myself is not exactly my own.'
deductions.inference: The visitor is using an alias.
deductions.conclusion: Holmes was already aware that 'Count Von Kramm' was not the visitor's true name.

deductions.observation: The visitor describes the matter as 'of such weight it may have an influence upon European history' and implicates 'one of the reigning families of Europe'. He then explicitly states it 'implicates the great House of Ormstein, hereditary kings of Bohemia.'
deductions.inference: Given the description of the case's importance and its impact on European royalty, it must involve a prominent royal house like the House of Ormstein.
deductions.conclusion: Holmes was already aware that the case involved the House of Ormstein.

deductions.observation: The client's gigantic stature, his uncontrollable agitation, his act of tearing a mask from his face, and the delicate nature of the case implicating the House of Ormstein.
deductions.inference: These characteristics, combined with the importance of the case, indicate a person of immense importance and royal lineage attempting to conceal their identity.
deductions.conclusion: The client is Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein, Grand Duke of Cassel-Felstein, and hereditary King of Bohemia.

deductions.observation: The King states that 'There is the writing' as proof of the letters' authenticity.
deductions.inference: The writing could be forged.
deductions.conclusion: The writing is not sufficient proof of authenticity.

deductions.observation: The King states 'My private note-paper' as proof of authenticity.
deductions.inference: The private note-paper could have been stolen.
deductions.conclusion: The private note-paper is not sufficient proof of authenticity.

deductions.observation: The King states 'My own seal' as proof of authenticity.
deductions.inference: The seal could have been imitated.
deductions.conclusion: The seal is not sufficient proof of authenticity.

deductions.observation: The King states 'My photograph' as proof of authenticity.
deductions.inference: The photograph could have been bought.
deductions.conclusion: The photograph is not sufficient proof of authenticity.

deductions.observation: The King states 'We were both in the photograph' as proof of authenticity.
deductions.inference: A photograph featuring both parties is much harder to dismiss or forge, making it strong evidence of their relationship.
deductions.conclusion: The King has committed a serious indiscretion by being photographed with Irene Adler.

deductions.observation: Irene Adler lives quietly, sings at concerts, drives out at five every day, and returns at seven sharp for dinner, seldom going out at other times except when she sings.
deductions.inference: Irene Adler has a regular and predictable daily routine.
deductions.conclusion: Her movements are largely scheduled and observable.

deductions.observation: Irene Adler has only one male visitor, Mr. Godfrey Norton, who is dark, handsome, and dashing, and calls never less than once a day, often twice.
deductions.inference: This frequent male visitor, Godfrey Norton, is highly significant to Irene Adler's situation.
deductions.conclusion: Godfrey Norton is an important factor in the matter.

deductions.observation: Godfrey Norton is a lawyer.
deductions.inference: The fact that he is a lawyer 'sounded ominous' to Holmes.
deductions.conclusion: His profession might indicate a legal entanglement or a strategic move related to the case.

deductions.observation: Godfrey Norton makes frequent visits to Irene Adler.
deductions.inference: There is a close and significant relationship between them.
deductions.conclusion: The exact nature of their relationship (client, friend, or mistress) needs to be determined.

deductions.observation: If Irene Adler were Godfrey Norton's client.
deductions.inference: She had probably transferred the photograph to his keeping.
deductions.conclusion: The photograph's location would likely be with Godfrey Norton.

deductions.observation: If Irene Adler were Godfrey Norton's mistress.
deductions.inference: It was less likely she had transferred the photograph to his keeping.
deductions.conclusion: The photograph's location would likely not be with Godfrey Norton.

deductions.observation: The relationship between Irene Adler and Godfrey Norton.
deductions.inference: On the issue of this question depended whether I should continue my work at Briony Lodge, or turn my attention to the...
deductions.conclusion: The next investigative step depends entirely on understanding their relationship.

deductions.observation: The gentleman is either Irene Adler's friend or her mistress.
deductions.inference: If he is her friend, she had probably transferred the photograph to his keeping. If he is her mistress, it was less likely.
deductions.conclusion: The location of the photograph (Briony Lodge or the gentleman's chambers in the Temple) depends on the nature of their relationship.

deductions.observation: It was twenty-five minutes to twelve, and Irene Adler offered a half sovereign to reach the Church of St. Monica in twenty minutes.
deductions.inference: The urgency and specific time frame indicate a time-sensitive event.
deductions.conclusion: It was clear enough what was in the wind, implying Holmes understood they were rushing to get married before a deadline.

deductions.observation: The photograph is cabinet size.
deductions.inference: It is too large for easy concealment about a woman's dress.
deductions.conclusion: It is unlikely she carries it about her person due to its physical dimensions.

deductions.observation: She knows that the King is capable of having her waylaid and searched, and two attempts of the sort have already been made.
deductions.inference: Given the known risks and past attempts, she would take precautions against being found with the photograph on her person.
deductions.conclusion: She does not carry the photograph about with her.

deductions.observation: The object is too large for easy concealment about a woman's dress.
deductions.inference: She knows that the King is capable of having her waylaid and searched, and two attempts of the sort have already been made.
deductions.conclusion: She does not carry it about with her.

deductions.observation: Considering the possibilities of her banker or her lawyer holding the object.
deductions.inference: Women are naturally secretive and like to do their own secreting. She could trust her own guardianship, but not the potential indirect or political influence on a business man.
deductions.conclusion: She would not hand it over to anyone else.

deductions.observation: She had resolved to use the object within a few days.
deductions.inference: It must be where she can lay her hands upon it easily.
deductions.conclusion: It must be in her own house.

deductions.observation: The house has twice been burgled.
deductions.inference: The previous burglars did not know how to look for the object.
deductions.conclusion: Holmes will not look for it, but will get her to show him.

deductions.observation: everyone in the street was an accomplice. They were all engaged for the evening.
deductions.inference: The crowd was part of a pre-arranged plan.
deductions.conclusion: The 'row' that broke out was a staged event to create a diversion.

deductions.observation: I had a little moist red paint in the palm of my hand. I rushed forward, fell down, clapped my hand to my face, and became a piteous spectacle.
deductions.inference: Holmes faked an injury using paint.
deductions.conclusion: This was a trick to gain sympathy and entry into the house.

deductions.observation: They carried me in. She was bound to have me in... And into her sitting-room, which was the very room which I suspected. It lay between that and her bedroom, and I was determined to see which.
deductions.inference: The woman was compelled to admit him due to his apparent injury, and he was taken to a room he already suspected.
deductions.conclusion: The ruse successfully placed him in a key location (the sitting-room).

deductions.observation: I motioned for air, they were compelled to open the window, and you had your chance.
deductions.inference: Holmes feigned needing air to get the window opened.
deductions.conclusion: Opening the window was a signal or opportunity for Watson to act (e.g., throw the smoke rocket).

deductions.observation: When a woman thinks that her house is on fire, her instinct is at once to rush to the thing which she values most. It is a perfectly overpowering impulse, and I have more than once taken advantage of it.
deductions.inference: This instinct is a reliable psychological principle.
deductions.conclusion: This principle can be used to discover the location of a hidden, valued object by simulating a fire.

deductions.observation: her instinct is at once to rush to the thing which she values most.
deductions.inference: It is a perfectly overpowering impulse
deductions.conclusion: This impulse can be exploited, as demonstrated in past cases like the Darlington Substitution Scandal and the Arnsworth Castle business.

deductions.observation: A married woman grabs at her baby; an unmarried one reaches for her jewel-box.
deductions.inference: our lady of to-day had nothing in the house more precious to her than what we are in quest of.
deductions.conclusion: She would rush to secure it.

deductions.observation: The alarm of fire was admirably done. The smoke and shouting were enough to shake nerves of steel. She responded beautifully.
deductions.conclusion: The photograph is in a recess behind a sliding panel just above the right bell-pull, as she was there in an instant and half drew it out.

deductions.observation: Irene Adler is married to an English lawyer named Norton.
deductions.inference: If Irene Adler loves her husband, she will not love the King. If she does not love the King, she will have no reason to interfere with his Majesty's plan.
deductions.conclusion: Her marriage to Norton is a hopeful development as it may spare the King all fear of future annoyance.

deductions.observation: The furniture was scattered about in every direction, with dismantled shelves and open drawers.
deductions.inference: The lady had hurriedly ransacked them.
deductions.conclusion: Irene Adler had ransacked the room before her flight.

scenes.title: Introduction to Holmes's Character and Irene Adler
scenes.description: On March 20, 1888, Watson returns from a patient visit and passes Holmes's brightly lit rooms on Baker Street, feeling a strong desire to see him again. | The narrator introduces Sherlock Holmes's unique character, his aversion to emotions, and his singular regard for Irene Adler. The narrator also mentions how his own marriage has created distance between them.

scenes.title: Arrival at St. Monica's and Norton's Plea
scenes.description: A gentleman arrives at Briony Lodge in a hansom cab, enters the house, paces excitedly in the sitting-room, and then departs in a hurry, giving instructions to the cabman to drive to Gross & Hankey's and then to the Church of St. Monica. | A street fight erupts involving guardsmen and loungers. Holmes intervenes to protect a lady, gets struck, and falls injured. The lady, identified as Irene Adler, then directs that Holmes be brought into Briony Lodge. | Holmes arrives at the Church of St. Monica to find Irene Adler, Godfrey Norton, and a clergyman. Norton urgently calls Holmes to participate in an event. | Holmes discusses with Watson the strategic decision of where to focus the investigation, depending on the relationship between Irene Adler and the gentleman and the potential location of the photograph. | Holmes gives detailed instructions for a plan involving a smoke-rocket and a cry of fire, then disappears to change into the character of an amiable and simple-minded Nonconformist clergyman. | Holmes, realizing the urgency, hails a cab and instructs the driver to follow Irene Adler to the Church of St. Monica, also offering a bonus for speed. | Irene Adler rushes out of the hall door and into a waiting landau, instructing the coachman to reach the Church of St. Monica in twenty minutes. | Sherlock Holmes, Watson, and the King read a letter from Irene Adler, where she explains how she discovered Holmes's disguise, her marriage, and her decision to flee with the photograph. | The elderly woman informs Holmes that Irene Adler has left England with her husband for the Continent. | Watson describes Holmes's reclusive nature, his habits including cocaine use, and his dedication to solving crimes, listing some of his past successful cases.

scenes.title: Watson visits Holmes at Baker Street
scenes.description: Dr. Watson, prompted by memories of past cases, visits Sherlock Holmes at his brilliantly lit rooms on Baker Street, finding him deeply engrossed in a new problem. Holmes immediately makes several personal observations and deductions about Watson's recent life.

scenes.title: Holmes deduces Watson's recent activities and profession
scenes.description: Holmes explains to Watson how he deduced Watson's recent country walk, his careless servant, and his medical profession based on subtle physical clues.

scenes.title: Conversation on Observation and Arrival of Note
scenes.description: Holmes explains the difference between seeing and observing to the narrator using the example of the steps in their residence. Following this, Holmes receives a mysterious, undated, and unsigned note inviting him to a consultation with a gentleman who may wear a mask.

scenes.title: Discussion of the Photograph's Location
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson are interrupted by the arrival of a very tall, richly dressed man wearing a black vizard mask, who has a German accent and has sent a note prior to his visit. | Holmes and Watson discuss the origin of a note, deducing the writer's nationality. They then hear the client arrive, and Holmes deduces the client's wealth from the sounds and sight of their carriage. | Holmes and Watson discuss the significance of the photograph, its potential impact on Mr. Godfrey Norton and the King, and deduce that the woman does not carry it on her person. | Holmes and the narrator discuss a mysterious note announcing a masked visitor, leading Holmes to deduce the origin of the paper. | Holmes discusses his plan for the evening with the Doctor, outlining their roles in an operation to take place at Briony Lodge when Miss Irene returns from her drive. | Holmes, the King, and Watson enter the ransacked drawing-room, where Holmes discovers a photograph and a letter. | Holmes, the King, and Watson read Irene Norton's letter, which resolves the potential scandal. The King expresses relief and offers Holmes a reward, which Holmes declines in favor of Irene's photograph. | Immediately after the gentleman's departure, a landau arrives at Briony Lodge, driven by a disheveled coachman.

scenes.title: Discussion of Irene Adler and the Compromising Letters
scenes.description: A mysterious visitor, 'Count Von Kramm', arrives at Holmes's residence, reveals his alias, and explains the delicate nature of his case, which involves the House of Ormstein and a potential immense scandal, requiring absolute secrecy from Holmes and Watson. | Holmes questions the King of Bohemia about his past entanglement with Irene Adler and the compromising letters, assessing the authenticity and implications of the evidence the King presents.

scenes.title: The King Reveals His Identity
scenes.description: The disguised client, initially referred to as Count Von Kramm, removes his mask and reveals his true identity as Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein, the hereditary King of Bohemia, explaining his reasons for seeking Holmes's help incognito. | The narrator is unexpectedly pulled into being a witness for the wedding of Irene Adler and Godfrey Norton at a church.

scenes.title: The King reveals the threat
scenes.description: The King explains the gravity of the situation regarding the compromising photograph with Irene Adler, her intentions, and the impending deadline before his marriage to Clotilde Lothman von Saxe-Meningen.

scenes.title: Holmes receives payment and address for investigation
scenes.description: Holmes discusses the case with the King (the Count Von Kramm) and Watson, receives payment for expenses, and obtains Mademoiselle's address. He then dismisses the King and asks Watson to return the next day.

scenes.title: Watson returns to Baker Street
scenes.description: Watson arrives at Baker Street at three o'clock the following afternoon as requested, but Holmes has not yet returned.

scenes.title: Watson Awaits Holmes at Baker Street
scenes.description: Holmes is carried into Briony Lodge, feigning injury. The narrator (Watson) then throws a smoke-rocket into the room, shouting 'Fire!' to create a diversion and observe Irene Adler's reaction. | Holmes, having changed his costume, and Watson leave Baker Street and arrive at Serpentine Avenue at dusk, observing the street activity outside Briony Lodge. | Holmes, the King, and Watson arrive at Briony Lodge and are greeted by an elderly woman. | Watson arrives at Baker Street at three o'clock to meet Holmes, who is not yet back. He waits by the fire, reflecting on Holmes's methods and the current case.

scenes.title: Holmes Returns in Disguise
scenes.description: Holmes returns to Baker Street shortly before four o'clock, disguised as a drunken groom. Watson recognizes him after a moment, and Holmes quickly changes into his usual attire, then laughs heartily.

scenes.title: Holmes recounts his reconnaissance
scenes.description: Holmes, after emerging from his bedroom, laughs heartily and then recounts his morning activities, including his disguise as a groom and his detailed observation of Briony Lodge and its surroundings.

scenes.title: Information Gathering at Serpentine-mews
scenes.description: Holmes, disguised as an ostler, gathers detailed information about Irene Adler's habits and her frequent visitor, Mr. Godfrey Norton, from the ostlers at the mews.

scenes.title: Strategic Reflection on Godfrey Norton
scenes.description: Holmes walks near Briony Lodge, reflecting on the significance of Mr. Godfrey Norton as a lawyer and frequent visitor, and how his relationship with Irene Adler impacts the search for the photograph and the overall investigation strategy.

scenes.title: Post-Wedding Departure
scenes.description: After the wedding, the narrator reflects on the event, and the newly married couple, Irene Adler and Godfrey Norton, separate to go their own ways, planning to meet later.

scenes.title: Holmes's Deduction on the Object's Location
scenes.description: Holmes and the King discuss Irene Adler's potential affections and their impact on the King's plans. | Holmes explains his reasoning for where the compromising photograph must be hidden, concluding it is in the lady's house, despite previous burglaries.

scenes.title: Arrival at Briony Lodge and Commotion
scenes.description: A carriage arrives at Briony Lodge, leading to a fierce quarrel among several men vying to open the door for the lady.

scenes.title: Holmes explains his ruse
scenes.description: Holmes and the Doctor leave the scene of the uproar and walk towards Edgeware Road, where Holmes explains the details of his staged injury and the psychological trick used to discover the photograph's location.

scenes.title: Planning the Photograph Retrieval
scenes.description: Holmes and the Doctor discuss the next steps, with Holmes outlining his plan to call with the King the following morning to retrieve the photograph. | Holmes describes to the Doctor how he orchestrated a false fire alarm to discover the hiding place of the photograph, observing the lady's instinctive reaction.

scenes.title: Discussion of the plan and return to Baker Street
scenes.description: Holmes and the narrator discuss the plan to call at 8 AM to retrieve the photograph, emphasizing promptness due to Irene Adler's potential marriage. They arrive at Baker Street.

scenes.title: Mysterious greeting at Baker Street
scenes.description: As Holmes searches his pockets for the key at Baker Street, a slim youth in an ulster greets him with 'Good-night, Mister Sherlock Holmes.' Holmes recognizes the voice but cannot identify the person.

scenes.title: King of Bohemia's impatient arrival
scenes.description: The narrator and Holmes are having breakfast when the King of Bohemia rushes into the room, eagerly asking if Holmes has retrieved the photograph.

scenes.title: Journey to Briony Lodge and revelation of marriage
scenes.description: Holmes, the narrator, and the King depart for Briony Lodge in the King's brougham. Holmes reveals that Irene Adler is married to an English lawyer named Norton and explains why this development is beneficial for the King.

scenes.title: Holmes Concludes Meeting with the King
scenes.description: Holmes requests and obtains Irene's photograph from the King, then departs for his chambers, reflecting on how his plans were beaten by Irene's wit.

events.name: Holmes Considers Godfrey Norton's Role
events.description: A note is received announcing an important, masked visitor. | A smart little landau carrying the lady rattles up to the door of Briony Lodge. | A tall, disguised man arrives at Holmes's residence, having previously sent a note, and is invited in. | During the fire alarm ruse, Holmes observes the lady rushing to a recess behind a sliding panel, revealing where the photograph is hidden. | Godfrey Norton urgently calls upon Holmes inside the Church of St. Monica, indicating a time-sensitive need for his presence. | Holmes analyzes the implications of Mr. Godfrey Norton's frequent visits and profession as a lawyer, realizing the nature of his relationship with Irene Adler is key to the investigation. | Holmes and the narrator examine the paper of the mysterious note, leading to deductions about its origin. | Holmes is struck during the scuffle while protecting a lady and falls to the ground, bleeding. | Holmes orchestrates a false fire alarm to provoke the lady into revealing the hiding place of the photograph. | Immediately after their wedding, Irene Adler and Godfrey Norton depart in different directions, with Irene stating her intention to drive in the park later. | Irene Adler leaves England with her husband by train for the Continent. | The client removes his mask and declares himself to be Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein, the King of Bohemia, confirming Holmes's prior deduction. | The gentleman departs Briony Lodge in a hansom cab, instructing the cabman to drive quickly to Gross & Hankey's and then to the Church of St. Monica. | The narrator's marriage has caused a drift in his relationship with Sherlock Holmes, absorbing his attention with home-centred interests.

events.name: Holmes's summons to Odessa for the Trepoff murder
events.description: Holmes was called to Odessa to investigate the Trepoff murder case.

events.name: Holmes clearing up the singular tragedy of the Atkinson brothers
events.description: Holmes successfully resolved the mysterious tragedy involving the Atkinson brothers at Trincomalee.

events.name: Holmes's mission for the reigning family of Holland
events.description: Holmes completed a delicate and successful mission for the royal family of Holland.

events.name: Watson's return to civil practice
events.description: Watson resumed his medical practice after his previous adventures.

events.name: Watson's visit to Baker Street on March 20, 1888
events.description: Watson passed Holmes's lodgings on Baker Street and felt a keen desire to see his old friend.

events.name: Watson's visit to Holmes
events.description: Dr. Watson, after reading about the 'Study in Scarlet,' visits Sherlock Holmes at his Baker Street rooms, finding him engrossed in a new problem and engaging in a series of personal deductions about Watson's life.

events.name: Holmes receives a mysterious note
events.description: A thick, pink-tinted notepaper arrives by post, containing an invitation for Holmes to consult with a gentleman on a matter of great importance.

events.name: Gentleman to consult Holmes
events.description: A gentleman, whose identity is to be concealed by a mask, is scheduled to consult Holmes at a quarter to eight o'clock on a matter of the deepest moment.

events.name: The client's arrival
events.description: The sound of horses' hoofs, grating wheels, a bell pull, and a heavy step indicate the client's arrival at Holmes's residence.

events.name: Count Von Kramm's arrival and request for secrecy
events.description: A masked visitor, identifying as Count Von Kramm, arrives at Holmes's residence and requests Holmes and Watson to be bound to absolute secrecy for two years regarding a matter of extreme importance.

events.name: Revelation of the potential scandal involving the House of Ormstein
events.description: The visitor reveals that the case involves a potential immense scandal that could compromise the great House of Ormstein, hereditary kings of Bohemia.

events.name: King of Bohemia's entanglement with Irene Adler
events.description: Five years ago, during a visit to Warsaw, the King of Bohemia became entangled with Irene Adler and wrote her compromising letters.

events.name: King seeks to retrieve compromising letters
events.description: The King of Bohemia is now desirous of getting back the compromising letters from Irene Adler to prevent a scandal.

events.name: The King's impending marriage
events.description: The King is about to be married to Clotilde Lothman von Saxe-Meningen, second daughter of the King of Scandinavia.

events.name: Irene Adler's threat
events.description: Irene Adler threatens to send the compromising photograph to the King's fiancée's family.

events.name: Deadline for sending the photograph
events.description: Irene Adler plans to send the photograph on the day the betrothal is publicly proclaimed, which will be next Monday.

events.name: King provides funds for investigation
events.description: The King gives Holmes a chamois leather bag containing three hundred pounds in gold and seven hundred in notes for his expenses.

events.name: Holmes receives Mademoiselle's address
events.description: Holmes is given the address 'Briony Lodge, Serpentine Avenue, St. John's Wood' for Mademoiselle.

events.name: Holmes confirms photograph type
events.description: Holmes asks and confirms that the compromising photograph is a 'cabinet' type.

events.name: Holmes asks Watson to return
events.description: Holmes asks Watson to call tomorrow afternoon at three o'clock to discuss the matter.

events.name: Watson returns to Baker Street
events.description: Watson arrives at Baker Street at three o'clock the next day, but Holmes has not yet returned.

events.name: Watson arrives at Baker Street
events.description: Watson arrives at Holmes's residence at three o'clock as arranged, but Holmes is not there.

events.name: Holmes returns in disguise
events.description: Holmes enters his room disguised as a drunken-looking groom, surprising Watson.

events.name: Holmes changes out of disguise
events.description: Holmes vanishes into his bedroom and emerges five minutes later, dressed in his usual respectable tweed suit.

events.name: Holmes's reconnaissance of Briony Lodge
events.description: Holmes disguised himself as a groom out of work and thoroughly examined Briony Lodge, noting its structure, windows, and surrounding mews, and interacting with ostlers.

events.name: Separation of Godfrey Norton and Irene Adler
events.description: A cry of 'Fire!' is raised, causing panic and smoke to fill the room, as part of Holmes's ruse. | A fight breaks out in the street involving guardsmen, loungers, and a scissors-grinder. | Godfrey Norton drives back to the Temple, and Irene Adler returns to her own house after their wedding. | Holmes pursues Irene Adler in a cab after realizing the urgency of her destination. | Holmes, in disguise, successfully obtains detailed information about Irene Adler's daily routine and her relationship with Mr. Godfrey Norton from the ostlers at Serpentine-mews. | Irene Adler and Godfrey Norton get married in an impromptu ceremony, with the narrator serving as an unexpected witness due to an informality with their license. | Sherlock Holmes finds a photograph of Irene Adler and a letter addressed to him hidden in the drawing-room. | The context strongly implies Irene Adler and Godfrey Norton are about to be married, given the church setting, clergyman, and urgency. | The narrator throws a smoke-rocket into the room at Holmes's signal, initiating the staged fire alarm.

events.name: Gentleman's Visit to Briony Lodge
events.description: A gentleman visits Briony Lodge, staying for about half an hour, exhibiting signs of agitation. | Irene Adler hastily departs in a landau, aiming to reach the Church of St. Monica quickly. | Irene Adler, the lady Holmes protected, directs that the injured Holmes be brought into Briony Lodge for care.

events.name: Landau Arrives at Briony Lodge
events.description: A fierce quarrel breaks out among loafers, guardsmen, and a scissors-grinder over who gets to open the carriage door for the lady. | A landau arrives at Briony Lodge shortly after the gentleman's departure, with a disheveled coachman. | Holmes and Watson arrive at Serpentine Avenue, taking up a position outside Briony Lodge.

events.name: Holmes Asks for Doctor's Co-operation
events.description: Holmes asks the Doctor for his help in an upcoming operation, implying it might involve breaking the law or risk of arrest.

events.name: Holmes Explains Plan for Briony Lodge
events.description: Holmes details his plan to the Doctor, instructing him to be at Briony Lodge at seven to observe a window and await a signal. | Holmes informs the Doctor of his plan to call with the King the next morning at eight to retrieve the photograph.

events.name: Holmes explains the smoke-rocket plan
events.description: Holmes instructs an unnamed person to throw a smoke-rocket into a window and raise a cry of fire as part of his plan.

events.name: Holmes disguises himself as a Nonconformist clergyman
events.description: Holmes transforms his appearance and manner to portray an amiable and simple-minded Nonconformist clergyman.

events.name: Holmes changes costume
events.description: Holmes changes his attire, adopting a new persona for his investigation.

events.name: Discussion about the photograph
events.description: Holmes and Watson discuss the implications of the photograph and its likely location.

events.name: Holmes carried into Briony Lodge
events.description: Holmes is brought into Briony Lodge, feigning injury as part of his plan.

events.name: Holmes declares false alarm
events.description: Holmes assures the panicked crowd that the alarm is false after the smoke has been deployed.

events.name: The row broke out
events.description: A staged commotion in the street, part of Holmes's plan to create a diversion.

events.name: Holmes carried into the house
events.description: After faking an injury, Holmes was carried into the woman's house by the accomplices.

events.name: Woman revealed photograph's location
events.description: The woman, believing her house was on fire, instinctively rushed to the photograph, thereby revealing its location to Holmes.

events.name: Holmes's Escape from the House
events.description: After the ruse, Holmes makes his excuses and escapes from the house, deciding to wait to secure the photograph due to the coachman's presence.

events.name: Mysterious greeting to Holmes
events.description: A slim youth in an ulster greets 'Mister Sherlock Holmes' outside Baker Street, and Holmes recognizes the voice but cannot identify the person.

events.name: King of Bohemia's urgent visit
events.description: The King of Bohemia rushes into Holmes's room at Baker Street, grasping Sherlock Holmes by the shoulders and eagerly asking if he has retrieved the photograph.

events.name: Irene Adler's marriage revealed
events.description: Holmes reveals to the King that Irene Adler married an English lawyer named Norton the previous day.

events.name: Irene Adler's Revelation and Departure
events.description: Irene Adler sends a letter to Sherlock Holmes, revealing that she saw through his disguise, married, and has fled the country with her husband, taking the compromising photograph with her.

events.name: Irene Norton's letter received
events.description: A letter from Irene Norton, _née_ Adler, is received, stating she will not use the compromising photograph against the King and has married another man.

events.name: King offers reward to Holmes
events.description: The King of Bohemia, relieved by the letter, offers Holmes an emerald snake ring as a reward.

events.name: Holmes requests Irene's photograph
events.description: Holmes declines the King's ring and instead requests Irene Norton's photograph as his reward.

events.name: Holmes obtains Irene's photograph
events.description: Holmes asks the King for Irene's photograph and receives it, concluding their immediate business.

events.name: Holmes's plans beaten by a woman's wit
events.description: Mr. Sherlock Holmes's best plans were thwarted by Irene Adler's cleverness, leading to a reflection on his changed view of women's intelligence.

events.name: Scandal threatens Bohemia
events.description: A great scandal is threatening to affect the kingdom of Bohemia, despite Holmes's efforts.

deductions.observation: The assistant promptly answers directions and closes the door.

deductions.observation: The knees of his trousers.

deductions.observation: Holmes fell upon his knees upon the floor and, with the lantern and a magnifying lens, began to examine minutely the cracks between the stones.
deductions.conclusion: We have at least an hour before us.

deductions.observation: Holmes minutely examined the cracks between the stones.
deductions.inference: The criminals are likely using these cracks to enter, and their activity is timed with the pawnbroker's sleep.
deductions.conclusion: We have at least an hour before us, for they can hardly take any steps until the good pawnbroker is safely in bed.

deductions.observation: The current location is the cellar of the City branch of one of the principal London banks.
deductions.inference: This specific bank cellar holds significant valuable assets.
deductions.conclusion: The more daring criminals of London should take a considerable interest in this cellar at present.

deductions.observation: The bank's reserve of bullion is much larger than usually kept in a single branch office, and the directors have had misgivings upon the subject.
deductions.inference: The large reserve and the directors' misgivings indicate a heightened risk of theft.
deductions.conclusion: Which were very well justified.

deductions.observation: the enemy's preparations have gone so far
deductions.inference: we cannot risk the presence of a light

deductions.observation: These are daring men
deductions.inference: they may do us some harm unless we are careful

deductions.observation: The layout of the bank and adjacent house
deductions.conclusion: They have but one retreat... That is back through the house into Saxe-Coburg Square.

deductions.observation: Jones has an inspector and two officers waiting at the front door.
deductions.conclusion: Then we have stopped all the holes.

deductions.observation: the advertisement of the League, and the copying of the _Encyclopædia_
deductions.inference: it was perfectly obvious from the first that the only possible object of this rather fantastic business... must be to get this not over-bright pawnbroker out of the way for a number of hours every day.
deductions.conclusion: The Red-Headed League employment was a ruse to remove the pawnbroker from his shop daily.

deductions.observation: the assistant having come for half wages
deductions.conclusion: he had some strong motive for securing the situation.

deductions.observation: The man's business was a small one, and there was nothing in his house which could account for such elaborate preparations, and such an expenditure as they were at.
deductions.conclusion: It must, then, be something out of the house.

deductions.observation: the assistant's fondness for photography, and his trick of vanishing into the cellar
deductions.conclusion: The cellar! There was the end of this tangled clue.

deductions.observation: I made inquiries as to this mysterious assistant and found that I had to deal with one of the coolest and most daring criminals in London.
deductions.inference: He was doing something in the cellar—something which took many hours a day for months on end.
deductions.conclusion: I could think of nothing save that he was running a tunnel to some other building.

deductions.observation: Holmes beats upon the pavement with his stick.
deductions.inference: He was ascertaining whether the cellar stretched out in front or behind.
deductions.conclusion: The cellar was not in front.

deductions.observation: The assistant's knees were worn, wrinkled, and stained.
deductions.inference: They spoke of those hours of burrowing.

deductions.observation: The City and Suburban Bank abutted on the friend's premises.
deductions.conclusion: Holmes had solved the problem of what they were burrowing for (the bank).

deductions.observation: The League offices closed.
deductions.inference: That was a sign that they cared no longer about Mr. Jabez Wilson's presence, meaning they had completed their tunnel.

deductions.observation: It was essential that they should use the tunnel soon, as it might be discovered or the bullion might be removed. Saturday would suit them better than any other day, as it would give them two days for their escape.
deductions.conclusion: Holmes expected them to come tonight (Saturday).

deductions.observation: Saturday would suit them better than any other day, as it would give them two days for their escape.
deductions.inference: To maximize their escape time over the weekend, the criminals would commit the crime on the night immediately preceding the weekend.
deductions.conclusion: I expected them to come to-night.

scenes.title: Mr. Wilson's Introduction to Spaulding and the Advertisement
scenes.description: Mr. Wilson describes his assistant, Spaulding, his habits including photography, and how Spaulding brought the advertisement for the Red-headed League to his attention, sparking Mr. Wilson's curiosity. | Watson calls upon Mr. Sherlock Holmes and finds him in conversation with Mr. Wilson. Holmes invites Watson to stay, introducing him as a partner and helper, and noting Watson's interest in unusual cases. | Watson expresses confusion and surprise after reading the extraordinary advertisement, while Holmes chuckles.

scenes.title: Discussion of Past Cases and Introduction of New Client
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson discuss the nature of their cases, with Holmes asserting that life is stranger than imagination. Mr. Jabez Wilson arrives to present a new, singular case, and Holmes asks him to recommence his narrative for Watson's benefit.

scenes.title: Client presents newspaper
scenes.description: The portly client, described as an obese, pompous, and slow British tradesman, pulls out a dirty and wrinkled newspaper from his greatcoat. Watson attempts to deduce information from the client's appearance but gains little, while Sherlock Holmes observes Watson's efforts.

scenes.title: Holmes's Initial Deductions about Jabez Wilson
scenes.description: Holmes explains to Watson and Mr. Wilson how he deduced aspects of Mr. Wilson's background based on observations like the Chinese coin and knowledge of fish scale staining. | Sherlock Holmes reveals his initial deductions about Mr. Jabez Wilson's past and habits, explaining his reasoning based on physical observations of his hands, clothing, and tattoos.

scenes.title: The Red-Headed League Advertisement
scenes.description: Candidates are interviewed by a small man; most are disqualified, but Mr. Jabez Wilson is accepted due to his vivid flame-coloured hair. | Mr. Wilson finds and presents a newspaper advertisement for the Red-Headed League, detailing the vacancy, salary, eligibility, and application instructions.

scenes.title: Client Presents Dissolution Notice
scenes.description: Holmes and the Doctor listen as Mr. Wilson starts to explain his situation, beginning with the advertisement and his business. | The client shows Holmes and Watson the cardboard notice announcing the dissolution of The Red-Headed League and recounts his attempts to find information about it and Mr. Duncan Ross, learning his real name was William Morris from the landlord. | While waiting in the dark vault, Watson observes a hand emerging from a hole in the floor, followed by a stone being removed and a face appearing, illuminated by a lantern, signaling the criminals' entry.

scenes.title: Mr. Wilson's Application for the Red-Headed League
scenes.description: Mr. Wilson recounts his experience applying for the Red-Headed League, describing the specific requirements for red hair and the overwhelming crowd of applicants in London.

scenes.title: Journey to the Red-Headed League Office
scenes.description: Spaulding and the client navigate a large crowd of red-headed individuals to reach the office for the advertisement.

scenes.title: Holmes listens to client's story
scenes.description: Holmes listens to his client, Mr. Jabez Wilson, recount his experience applying for the Red-Headed League vacancy.

scenes.title: Vacancy Announcement and Crowd Dispersal
scenes.description: Holmes and Jones confront the intruders emerging from the tunnel. Holmes captures John Clay, while his accomplice, Archie, escapes. | Jabez Wilson returns home, consults his assistant without success, and decides to seek advice from Holmes. | Jabez Wilson returns home, reflects on the unusual job, and discusses his doubts with Vincent Spaulding, fearing it might be a hoax. | Mr. Duncan Ross announces from a window that the vacancy is filled, leading to the dispersal of other red-headed applicants. | Mr. Duncan Ross examines and tugs Mr. Wilson's hair to verify its authenticity for the Red-Headed League position, then congratulates him. | Mr. Duncan Ross explains the terms of the copying job to Mr. Jabez Wilson, who accepts the position. | Mr. Merryweather and the narrator discuss John Clay's criminal reputation and background. The group then prepares to depart in hansoms. | Watson reflects on Holmes's superior understanding of the case and drives home to Kensington, pondering the upcoming nocturnal expedition.

scenes.title: Inquiry into Marital Status
scenes.description: Mr. Duncan Ross questions Mr. Wilson about his marital status and family, expressing concern about him being a bachelor in relation to the fund's purpose.

scenes.title: Mr. Wilson recounts Red-Headed League job offer
scenes.description: Mr. Wilson explains to Mr. Holmes the details of the job offer he received from the Red-Headed League, including the strict conditions and the roles of Vincent Spaulding and Mr. Duncan Ross.

scenes.title: Preparation for Work
scenes.description: Despite his doubts, Jabez Wilson decides to proceed with the job, purchasing supplies and heading to Pope's Court.

scenes.title: Holmes's Initial Assessment of the Assistant
scenes.description: Holmes acknowledges the remarkable nature of the case and suggests it might involve graver issues than initially apparent, while also noting Jabez Wilson's financial gain. | Holmes and the Doctor emerge from St. James's Hall, and Holmes informs the Doctor about a serious business at Coburg Square, revealing a considerable crime is in contemplation and requesting his help for that night. | Holmes asks the assistant for directions to the Strand, then comments on his intelligence and daring to Watson, revealing he has known something of him before. | Jabez Wilson arrives at Pope's Court, finds everything ready, and begins copying the _Encyclopædia Britannica_ under the supervision of Mr. Duncan Ross. | Mr. Merryweather guides Holmes and the group through a series of gates and passages into a large underground vault. Holmes immediately begins to examine the structural integrity and the floor for clues, while Mr. Merryweather inadvertently reveals the hollowness of the floor. | Watson deduces Holmes's true motive for asking directions was to see the assistant, but Holmes corrects him, stating he was interested in the assistant's trousers and saw what he expected.

scenes.title: Narrator's Account of Red-Headed League Work and Termination
scenes.description: The narrator describes his daily routine working for the Red-Headed League, the supervision by Mr. Duncan Ross, the regular payments, and the sudden, unexpected termination of his employment after eight weeks, culminating in finding the office door locked with a notice.

scenes.title: Client's Account of William Morris's Departure
scenes.description: Jabez Wilson recounts to Holmes how William Morris, the man at No. 4, moved out and gave him a new address.

scenes.title: Investigation at King Edward Street
scenes.description: Jabez Wilson's attempt to find William Morris at the given address, only to discover it's a manufactory and no one knows Morris or Ross. | Watson arrives at Baker Street to find Holmes in conversation with Peter Jones of Scotland Yard and Mr. Merryweather, completing their party for the night's adventure.

scenes.title: Holmes and Watson discuss the case
scenes.description: After Mr. Wilson leaves, Holmes and Watson discuss the mysterious nature of the case, with Holmes stating his philosophy on bizarre vs. commonplace crimes.

scenes.title: Holmes's 'three pipe problem'
scenes.description: Holmes curls up in his chair, smoking his pipe, entering a deep state of thought for fifty minutes to solve the problem, before suddenly springing up with a plan.

scenes.title: Holmes invites Watson to a concert
scenes.description: Holmes invites Watson to attend a Sarasate concert at St. James's Hall, suggesting they walk through the City and have lunch beforehand.

scenes.title: Hansom Ride to Farrington Street
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson travel by Underground to Aldersgate and then walk to Saxe-Coburg Square. | Holmes, Watson, Merryweather, and Jones travel in hansoms through gas-lit streets, with Holmes humming tunes, until they reach Farrington Street. | Watson leaves his home at a quarter-past nine and travels through the Park and Oxford Street to Baker Street.

scenes.title: Holmes's Investigation at Saxe-Coburg Square
scenes.description: Holmes inspects the pawnbroker's shop and its surroundings, thumps the pavement with his stick, and tests the assistant by asking for directions.

scenes.title: Exploring the City's Arteries
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson walk away from Saxe-Coburg Square, observing the stark contrast between the quiet square and the bustling main streets of the City, which are filled with traffic and pedestrians. Holmes begins to memorize the order of the houses.

scenes.title: Holmes surveys the street
scenes.description: Holmes stands at a corner, observing and listing the businesses along the street, demonstrating his hobby of knowing London.

scenes.title: Holmes suggests leisure
scenes.description: After their work, Holmes suggests a break for a sandwich, coffee, and then playing the violin, expressing his desire for harmony away from client conundrums.

scenes.title: Narrator reflects on Holmes's character
scenes.description: The narrator describes Holmes's dual nature, contrasting his intense investigative persona with his contemplative, musical side, particularly when playing the violin.

scenes.title: Watson's Reflection on Holmes's Intellect
scenes.description: The Doctor reflects on his own perceived stupidity in comparison to Sherlock Holmes's ability to foresee events based on observations.

scenes.title: Pre-adventure Briefing
scenes.description: Holmes, Watson, Mr. Jones, and Mr. Merryweather gather before embarking on their adventure, discussing the stakes and the target.

scenes.title: Arrival at the Thoroughfare
scenes.description: The group arrives at a crowded thoroughfare, dismisses their cabs, and prepares to proceed on foot.

scenes.title: Waiting in the Bank Cellar
scenes.description: Holmes, Mr. Merryweather, and the Doctor are waiting in the bank cellar, discussing the impending theft of the French gold and making preparations to confront the criminals. | Holmes, Watson, Mr. Merryweather, and Jones wait in pitch darkness within the bank vault, preparing to ambush the criminals. Holmes gives instructions for positioning and warns of potential danger.

scenes.title: Arrest of John Clay and Mr. Merryweather's gratitude
scenes.description: John Clay is arrested and makes defiant remarks. Mr. Merryweather expresses gratitude to Holmes for preventing the bank robbery.

scenes.title: Holmes explains the Red-Headed League's true purpose
scenes.description: Holmes explains to Watson in Baker Street that the Red-Headed League was a scheme to get the pawnbroker out of his shop daily.

scenes.title: Holmes explains his deductions to Watson
scenes.description: Holmes recounts his investigative steps, including examining the cellar, observing the assistant's knees, identifying the bank as the target, and predicting the timing of the crime.

events.name: Mr. Jabez Wilson calls upon Holmes
events.description: Mr. Jabez Wilson arrives at Holmes's residence to present his case. | Watson visits Mr. Sherlock Holmes one day in the autumn of last year.

events.name: Holmes introduces Watson to Mr. Wilson
events.description: Holmes introduces Watson to his new client, Mr. Wilson, emphasizing Watson's role as a partner and helper in his cases.

events.name: Holmes asks Mr. Wilson to recommence his narrative
events.description: Holmes requests Mr. Wilson to retell his story from the beginning for Dr. Watson.

events.name: Discovery of the Red-Headed League Advertisement
events.description: Holmes begins his detailed inspection of the vault's structure and floor, making observations about its security and the timing of potential criminal activity, while Mr. Merryweather's actions reveal the hollowness of the floor. | Mr. Jabez Wilson presents the newspaper advertisement that initiated his involvement with the Red-Headed League, which offers a salary for nominal services to red-headed men. | Sherlock Holmes reveals the high stakes of the night's undertaking: £30,000 for Mr. Merryweather and the capture of John Clay for Mr. Jones.

events.name: Advertisement in The Morning Chronicle
events.description: An advertisement published on April 27, 1890, which had a significant effect on Jabez Wilson's fortunes.

events.name: Spaulding discovers the Red-headed League advertisement
events.description: Spaulding comes into Mr. Wilson's office with a newspaper advertisement for the League of the Red-headed Men.

events.name: Spaulding expresses interest in the Red-headed League
events.description: Spaulding tells Mr. Wilson he wishes he were red-headed to qualify for a vacancy in the League, highlighting its financial benefits.

events.name: Mr. Wilson learns about the Red-headed League
events.description: Mr. Wilson, being a stay-at-home man, asks Spaulding for details about the Red-headed League after seeing the advertisement.

events.name: Founding of the League of the Red-headed Men
events.description: The League was founded by American millionaire Ezekiah Hopkins to provide easy berths for red-headed men.

events.name: Public Knowledge of Unpacked Gold
events.description: Holmes introduces Mr. Merryweather to Watson and Mr. Jones as their companion for the night's adventure. | It became known that the borrowed 30,000 napoleons were never unpacked and are still lying in the bank's cellar. | John Clay is arrested and handcuffed by Jones. | John Clay is identified as the notorious criminal target, described as a murderer, thief, smasher, and forger. | The bank borrowed 30,000 napoleons from the Bank of France to strengthen its resources some months ago. | The landlord reveals to the client that the man known as Mr. Duncan Ross was actually William Morris, a solicitor using the room temporarily. | Upon his death, Ezekiah Hopkins left his fortune to trustees with instructions to apply the interest to the League of the Red-headed Men.

events.name: Application for the Red-Headed League
events.description: Mr. Wilson, encouraged by Vincent Spaulding, applies for a position advertised by the Red-Headed League, encountering a massive crowd of other red-headed men.

events.name: Application for Red-Headed League vacancy
events.description: The client, Mr. Jabez Wilson, applies for a vacancy advertised by the Red-Headed League.

events.name: Mr. Jabez Wilson's acceptance into the League
events.description: Mr. Jabez Wilson is accepted into the Red-Headed League due to his red hair after an interview process.

events.name: Vacancy Filled Announcement
events.description: Mr. Duncan Ross physically tests Mr. Wilson's hair by tugging it to ensure it is real. | Mr. Duncan Ross questions Mr. Wilson about his marital status and family, revealing a preference for married men with families for the fund. | Mr. Duncan Ross shouts from the window that the Red-Headed League vacancy has been filled, causing other applicants to leave.

events.name: Mr. Wilson's Red-Headed League Job Offer and Conditions
events.description: Mr. Wilson recounts receiving a job offer from the Red-Headed League, facilitated by Vincent Spaulding and explained by Mr. Duncan Ross, detailing the nominal work, £4 weekly pay, and strict requirement to remain in the office from ten to two.

events.name: Jabez Wilson is offered the position
events.description: Mr. Duncan Ross offers Jabez Wilson a peculiar job copying the _Encyclopædia Britannica_ for The Red-Headed League.

events.name: Jabez Wilson doubts the job's legitimacy
events.description: After accepting the job, Jabez Wilson becomes suspicious that the offer might be a hoax or fraud due to its unusual nature and high pay for simple work.

events.name: Jabez Wilson decides to proceed with the job
events.description: Despite his doubts, Jabez Wilson determines to go through with the job and prepares for his first day.

events.name: Jabez Wilson commences copying the _Encyclopædia Britannica_
events.description: Jabez Wilson starts his work at Pope's Court, copying from the _Encyclopædia Britannica_ under the watchful eye of Mr. Duncan Ross.

events.name: Start of Red-Headed League employment
events.description: After eight weeks, the narrator found the office door locked with a notice, signifying the sudden end of his employment with the Red-Headed League. | The narrator began working for the Red-Headed League, writing about various topics starting with 'A'.

events.name: Weekly payment received
events.description: The narrator received four golden sovereigns weekly for his work at the Red-Headed League.

events.name: Mr. Duncan Ross's reduced visits
events.description: Mr. Duncan Ross gradually reduced his visits to the office, eventually stopping altogether.

events.name: The Red-Headed League is dissolved
events.description: An announcement on a cardboard notice states that 'THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE IS DISSOLVED' on October 9, 1890.

events.name: Discovery of the dissolution notice
events.description: The client finds a cardboard notice on the door of the Red-Headed League office, announcing its dissolution.

events.name: Client's investigation into the League and Mr. Duncan Ross
events.description: After finding the dissolution notice, the client attempts to gather information from nearby offices and the landlord about the Red-Headed League and Mr. Duncan Ross.

events.name: William Morris moves out
events.description: William Morris vacates the room at No. 4, giving Jabez Wilson a new, false address.

events.name: Discovery of the manufactory at 17 King Edward Street
events.description: Jabez Wilson finds that the address given by William Morris is a manufactory of artificial knee-caps, and neither Morris nor Duncan Ross are known there.

events.name: Jabez Wilson loses Red-Headed League employment
events.description: The Red-Headed League employment, which provided Jabez Wilson with four pounds a week, abruptly ends.

events.name: Holmes decides to be prompt
events.description: Holmes states that he must be prompt in addressing the mysterious business of Mr. Wilson.

events.name: Holmes enters a period of intense thought
events.description: Holmes dedicates fifty minutes to deep contemplation, referring to the case as a 'three pipe problem', to formulate a plan.

events.name: Holmes invites Watson to a concert
events.description: Holmes invites Watson to accompany him to a Sarasate concert at St. James's Hall, planning to go through the City first.

events.name: Holmes and Watson travel to Saxe-Coburg Square
events.description: Holmes and Watson take the Underground to Aldersgate and walk to Saxe-Coburg Square to investigate the scene of the Red-Headed League employment.

events.name: Holmes investigates the pawnbroker's shop
events.description: Holmes meticulously examines the exterior of Jabez Wilson's pawnbroker's shop and the surrounding street, thumping the pavement with his stick.

events.name: Holmes tests the pawnbroker's assistant
events.description: Holmes asks the assistant for directions to the Strand, observing his prompt and intelligent response.

events.name: Holmes questions the assistant
events.description: Holmes asks Mr. Wilson's assistant for directions to the Strand.

events.name: Holmes assesses the assistant's intelligence
events.description: Holmes comments on the assistant's promptness and intelligence to Watson.

events.name: Holmes reveals interest in the assistant's trousers
events.description: Holmes clarifies to Watson that his true interest was in the assistant's trousers, not the assistant himself.

events.name: Holmes and Watson explore the City
events.description: Holmes and Watson walk through the busy streets of the City after leaving Saxe-Coburg Square.

events.name: Holmes memorizes house order
events.description: Holmes begins to remember the order of the houses on the street they are observing.

events.name: Holmes lists local businesses
events.description: Holmes recites the order of businesses on the street, including Mortimer's, a newspaper shop, the Coburg Bank, a Vegetarian Restaurant, and McFarlane's depot.

events.name: Holmes suggests a break
events.description: Holmes proposes a sandwich, coffee, and violin playing as a form of relaxation after their work.

events.name: Holmes plays the violin
events.description: Holmes spends the afternoon playing the violin, finding perfect happiness and displaying his musical talent.

events.name: Narrator describes Holmes's dual nature
events.description: The narrator provides an insight into Holmes's character, highlighting the contrast between his sharp investigative mind and his poetic, contemplative, and languid moods.

events.name: Holmes reveals a planned crime
events.description: Holmes informs the Doctor that a considerable crime is in contemplation at Coburg Square.

events.name: Holmes requests Watson's assistance
events.description: Holmes asks the Doctor to join him that night at Baker Street at ten o'clock, advising him to bring his army revolver due to potential danger.

events.name: Preparation for Nocturnal Expedition
events.description: Holmes arranges plans to confront the criminals, including covering a dark lantern and preparing to wait in darkness. | Holmes prepares for an upcoming nocturnal expedition by buttoning his pea-jacket and taking his heavy hunting crop, while introducing Mr. Merryweather to Watson and Peter Jones. | Holmes, Watson, Mr. Merryweather, and Jones take positions in the dark bank vault, preparing to ambush the criminals. Holmes instructs them to be ready to fire if necessary.

events.name: Discussion of John Clay's Criminality
events.description: Mr. Merryweather and the narrator discuss John Clay's exceptional criminal skills and elusive nature.

events.name: Departure for the Bank
events.description: Holmes, Watson, Mr. Merryweather, and Jones leave in two hansoms to reach their destination, presumably the bank.

events.name: Arrival at the Destination Thoroughfare
events.description: The group arrives at a busy street, dismisses their cabs, and prepares to continue their investigation.

events.name: Entry of the Criminals into the Vault
events.description: A broad, white stone is turned over, revealing a gaping hole from which a lantern light streams, and a clean-cut, boyish face peeks through. | The group, led by Mr. Merryweather, navigates through a narrow passage, side door, iron gates, and winding stone steps to reach a huge underground vault or cellar.

events.name: Appearance of the Hand from the Floor
events.description: A white, almost womanly hand emerges from a lurid spark on the stone pavement, feeling about the area.

events.name: Intruders emerge from the tunnel
events.description: A clean-cut, boyish face, followed by a companion with red hair, emerges from a hole.

events.name: Holmes captures John Clay
events.description: Sherlock Holmes springs out and seizes John Clay, disarming him of a revolver.

events.name: Archie escapes
events.description: John Clay's companion, Archie, dives back down the hole and escapes.

events.name: Holmes explains the Red-Headed League scheme
events.description: Holmes explains to Watson the true purpose of the Red-Headed League's advertisement and the copying of the Encyclopædia.

events.name: Holmes's initial investigation at the scene
events.description: Holmes visits the premises, beats the pavement to check the cellar's extent, and observes the assistant's worn knees.

events.name: Identification of the target bank
events.description: Holmes walks around the corner and realizes the City and Suburban Bank abuts the premises, identifying it as the target of the tunnel.

events.name: Closure of the Red-Headed League offices
events.description: The League offices close, signaling to Holmes that the tunnel is complete and the criminals are ready to act.

events.name: Holmes alerts authorities
events.description: Holmes contacts Scotland Yard and the chairman of the bank directors to prepare for the impending crime.

events.name: Prediction of the crime's timing
events.description: Holmes deduces that the criminals will make their attempt tonight (Saturday) due to the tunnel's completion and the advantage of a weekend escape.

crimes.name: Threat to Helen Stoner
crimes.description: An ongoing threat to Miss Stoner, implied by her reaction to Dr. Roylott following her. | Dr. Grimesby Roylott's attempt to murder Miss Stoner using a trained snake. | Dr. Roylott has followed Miss Stoner, causing her to fear for her safety. | Dr. Roylott's aggressive behavior and threats towards Holmes, stemming from Miss Stoner's visit, indicate an ongoing threat related to the case. | Helen Stoner's vague fears and suspicions about dangers encompassing her, which she asks Holmes to advise her on. | Holmes expresses concern that 'our little friend will not suffer from her imprudence in allowing this brute to trace her', indicating an ongoing threat to Miss Stoner. | Holmes warns the narrator that the least sound could be fatal to their plans and that their very life may depend on staying awake, indicating an active and immediate danger. | The 'subtle and horrible crime' that Holmes and Watson are trying to prevent. | The client heard the low whistle again, which was a herald of her sister's death, indicating a new threat to her. | The client hears a low whistle, similar to one heard before her sister's death, indicating an ongoing threat. | The client's current 'trouble' which she has confided to Holmes. | The doctor's interest in preventing his stepdaughter's marriage, implying a threat to Helen Stoner. | The ongoing dangers threatening Miss Stoner, which Holmes promises to drive away. | The ongoing threat to Helen Stoner's life, which Holmes is investigating. | The ongoing threat to Miss Stoner's life, which Holmes emphasizes is very serious. | The ongoing threat to Miss Stoner's life, which Holmes is investigating. | The ongoing threat to Miss Stoner, which is resolved by Dr. Roylott's death.

crimes.name: Death of Julia Stoner
crimes.description: Julia Stoner died without recovering consciousness. She was found in her night-dress with a charred match stump and a match-box. The coroner found no satisfactory cause of death, no marks of violence, and no poison. Helen believes she died of pure fear and nervous shock. | La narradora describe la noche en que su hermana Julia murió, escuchando un grito y un silbido. | Miss Stoner's sister met her fate in the second chamber, which is now Miss Stoner's current room. | The client's sister died in her bed, possibly from fear or nervous shock, and the client is now sleeping in the same bed. | The client's sister's death, preceded by a low whistle. | The death of Julia Stoner two years prior, which her sister Helen wishes to discuss with Sherlock Holmes, implying suspicious circumstances. | The death of Miss Stoner's sister, which Holmes is investigating, specifically focusing on the circumstances involving a ventilator and a cord. | The death of Miss Stoner's sister, which Holmes was hired to investigate. | The fate that Miss Stoner's sister met in the second chamber. | The financial implications of the 'will of the deceased wife' (Julia Stoner) are analyzed, providing a potential motive for her death or the threat to her sister. | The murder of Miss Stoner's sister, Julia Stoner, by Dr. Grimesby Roylott using a trained snake. | The mysterious death of Miss Stoner's sister, which Holmes is investigating. | The mysterious end of Helen Stoner's sister, referred to as 'her mysterious end' and 'dying woman'. | The mysterious end of the client's sister, which Holmes is investigating. | The past death of Helen Stoner's sister, which is connected to the current investigation. | The past death of a lady who slept in the bed, now understood to be connected to the ventilator and cord. | The past event that Holmes was investigating, linked to the 'band'. | The sudden and violent death of Helen's sister, Julia, who screams about 'the speckled band' before dying. | The terrible event that occurred a fortnight before Julia's wedding, depriving Helen of her only companion.
