deductions.observation: young ladies wander about the metropolis at this hour of the morning, and knock sleepy people up out of their beds
deductions.inference: Such unusual and urgent behavior indicates a serious matter.
deductions.conclusion: it is something very pressing which they have to communicate.

deductions.observation: I observe that you are shivering.
deductions.inference: The shivering is not caused by cold.
deductions.conclusion: The shivering is caused by fear, Mr. Holmes. It is terror.

deductions.observation: I observe the second half of a return ticket in the palm of your left glove.
deductions.inference: The lady traveled by train.
deductions.conclusion: You have come in by train this morning.

deductions.observation: The lady has a return ticket and came by train.
deductions.inference: To reach the station for an early train, she must have started early and used another form of transport.
deductions.conclusion: You must have started early, and yet you had a good drive in a dog-cart, along heavy roads, before you reached the station.

deductions.observation: The left arm of your jacket is spattered with mud in no less than seven places. The marks are perfectly fresh.
deductions.inference: There is no vehicle save a dog-cart which throws up mud in that way, and then only when you sit on the left-hand side of the driver.
deductions.conclusion: You drove in a dog-cart, along heavy roads, before you reached the station, sitting on the left-hand side of the driver.

deductions.observation: In her right hand was found the charred stump of a match, and in her left a match-box.
deductions.inference: She had struck a light and looked about her when the alarm took place.
deductions.conclusion: That is important.

deductions.observation: Holmes pushed back the frill of black lace which fringed the hand that lay upon our visitor's knee. Five little livid spots, the marks of four fingers and a thumb, were printed upon the white wrist.
deductions.inference: The marks on the wrist are consistent with being gripped forcefully by a hand.
deductions.conclusion: The client has been cruelly used/physically abused.

deductions.observation: the lady is correct in saying that the flooring and walls are sound, and that the door, window, and chimney are impassable
deductions.conclusion: her sister must have been undoubtedly alone when she met her mysterious end.

deductions.observation: nocturnal whistles
deductions.inference: What becomes, then, of these nocturnal whistles?

deductions.observation: the very peculiar words of the dying woman
deductions.inference: what of the very peculiar words of the dying woman?

deductions.observation: The nocturnal whistles, the peculiar words of the dying woman, the presence of a band of gipsies who are on intimate terms with the old doctor, the doctor's interest in preventing his stepdaughter's marriage, the dying allusion to a band, and Miss Helen Stoner hearing a metallic clang possibly caused by metal bars securing shutters.
deductions.inference: These combined observations suggest a coherent explanation for the mystery.
deductions.conclusion: There is good ground to think that the mystery may be cleared along those lines.

deductions.observation: The brute seized the poker and bent it into a curve with his huge brown hands.
deductions.inference: The brute possesses immense physical strength.

deductions.observation: The brute snarled, and hurling the twisted poker into the fireplace he strode out of the room.
deductions.inference: The brute is prone to violent outbursts and intimidation.

deductions.observation: The brute had the insolence to confound Holmes with the official detective force!
deductions.inference: The brute holds the official police in contempt and attempts to intimidate Holmes by associating him with them.
deductions.conclusion: This incident gives zest to the investigation.

deductions.observation: Holmes picked up the steel poker and, with a sudden effort, straightened it out again.
deductions.conclusion: Holmes's grip and strength are comparable to the brute's.

deductions.observation: Holmes returned from his excursion holding a sheet of blue paper, scrawled over with notes and figures, and stated, 'I have seen the will of the deceased wife.'
deductions.inference: Holmes has successfully obtained and reviewed the legal document pertaining to the inheritance.

deductions.observation: The will states that the total income, which at the time of the wife's death was little short of £1,100, is now, through the fall in agricultural prices, not more than £750. Each daughter can claim an income of £250, in case of marriage.
deductions.inference: If both daughters married, the brute's income would be reduced to £250. If even one married, his income would be reduced to £500.
deductions.conclusion: The brute has a strong financial motive to prevent the daughters from marrying.

deductions.observation: a lady is walking
deductions.inference: I fancy, is Miss Stoner
deductions.conclusion: And the lady, I fancy, is Miss Stoner

deductions.observation: the driver might gossip about their visit
deductions.inference: if the driver thinks we are architects or on definite business, it may stop his gossip
deductions.conclusion: I thought it as well that this fellow should think we had come here as architects, or on some definite business. It may stop his gossip.

deductions.observation: There does not seem to be any very pressing need for repairs at that end wall.
deductions.inference: The stated reason for alterations (repairs) is questionable.
deductions.conclusion: The alterations might be an excuse to move Miss Stoner from her room.

deductions.observation: The windows are very small ones, too narrow for anyone to pass through.
deductions.conclusion: No one could pass through these windows.

deductions.observation: Both Miss Stoner and her sister locked their doors at night.
deductions.conclusion: Their rooms were unapproachable from the corridor side.

deductions.observation: Holmes endeavoured in every way to force the shutter open, but without success.
deductions.conclusion: The shutters cannot be forced open from the outside.

deductions.observation: There was no slit through which a knife could be passed to raise the bar.
deductions.conclusion: The bar securing the shutters cannot be raised from the outside with a knife.

deductions.observation: Holmes tested the hinges and found them to be of solid iron, built firmly into the massive masonry.
deductions.conclusion: The hinges are extremely secure and cannot be easily tampered with.

deductions.observation: Based on the combined evidence from the shutters, bar, and hinges, no one could pass these shutters if they were bolted.
deductions.inference: This contradicts or complicates Holmes's initial theory about how someone might have entered or exited the room.
deductions.conclusion: His current theory certainly presents some difficulties.

deductions.observation: A thick bell-rope hung down beside the bed, the tassel actually lying upon the pillow.
deductions.inference: The bell-rope is positioned unusually close to the bed and seems to be for immediate use.

deductions.observation: The bell-rope 'looks newer than the other things'.
deductions.inference: The bell-rope was installed recently.
deductions.conclusion: The bell-rope was 'only put there a couple of years ago'.

deductions.observation: Miss Stoner states her sister never used the bell-rope and they 'used always to get what we wanted for ourselves'.
deductions.inference: The bell-rope was not installed for its stated purpose of calling the housekeeper, nor was it used by Julia Stoner.
deductions.conclusion: It seemed unnecessary to put so nice a bell-pull there.

deductions.observation: Holmes threw himself down upon his face with his lens in his hand and crawled swiftly backward and forward, examining minutely the cracks between the boards.
deductions.inference: Holmes is looking for minute details or evidence hidden within the floorboards.

deductions.observation: Holmes did the same with the wood-work.
deductions.inference: Holmes is looking for minute details or evidence hidden within the woodwork.

deductions.observation: Holmes examines minutely the cracks between the boards on the floor.
Holmes examines the woodwork with which the chamber was panelled.
Holmes stares at the bed and runs his eye up and down the wall.
The bell-rope is a dummy and not attached to a wire.
deductions.conclusion: The bell-rope cannot ring.

deductions.observation: The bell-rope is fastened to a hook just above the little opening for the ventilator.
The ventilator opens into another room, not to the outside air.
deductions.inference: A builder would be a fool to open a ventilator into another room instead of outside.

deductions.observation: The dummy bell-rope and the non-ventilating ventilator were installed around the same time.
deductions.conclusion: These features are of a 'most interesting character' and suggest a deliberate, unusual purpose.

deductions.observation: Holmes taps the safe and asks 'What's in here?'. Miss Stoner replies 'My stepfather's business papers.' Holmes asks 'Oh! you have seen inside, then?' Miss Stoner replies 'Only once, some years ago. I remember that it was full of papers.'
deductions.inference: Miss Stoner's knowledge of the safe's contents is limited and outdated.
deductions.conclusion: The safe's current contents are unknown to Miss Stoner.

deductions.observation: Holmes asks 'There isn't a cat in it, for example?' Miss Stoner replies 'No. What a strange idea!'
deductions.inference: Holmes is probing for the presence of an animal, possibly a cat, in an unusual place like the safe.
deductions.conclusion: There is no cat in the safe.

deductions.observation: Holmes takes up a small saucer of milk which stood on the top of the safe. Miss Stoner states, 'No; we don't keep a cat. But there is a cheetah and a baboon.'
deductions.inference: The presence of milk suggests an animal that drinks milk, but the stated animals (cheetah, baboon) are not typical milk-drinkers from a saucer, and a cheetah would require more. This creates a discrepancy.
deductions.conclusion: The saucer of milk is for an animal, but not necessarily the cheetah or baboon, or it's an insufficient amount for a cheetah, suggesting another, smaller animal.

deductions.observation: Holmes squatted down in front of the wooden chair and examined the seat of it with the greatest attention. He then says, 'Thank you. That is quite settled.'
deductions.inference: Holmes found a significant clue or piece of evidence on the seat of the wooden chair.
deductions.conclusion: The wooden chair's seat holds a resolved clue relevant to the case.

deductions.observation: Holmes finds a small dog lash hung on one corner of the bed. The lash was curled upon itself and tied so as to make a loop of whipcord.
deductions.inference: The dog lash is not merely a common object but has been deliberately modified by being tied into a loop of whipcord.
deductions.conclusion: The tied dog lash is an unusual and potentially significant object.

deductions.observation: Watson comments, 'It's a common enough lash. But I don't know why it should be tied.' Holmes responds, 'That is not quite so common, is it? Ah, me! it's a wicked world, and when a clever man turns his brains to crime it is the worst of all.'
deductions.inference: The unusual tying of the lash suggests a deliberate, possibly malicious, purpose, indicating a 'clever man' involved in 'crime.'
deductions.conclusion: The tied dog lash is a tool or instrument used by a clever criminal.

deductions.observation: Miss Stoner asks if her sister died from some sudden fright.
deductions.inference: Holmes considers the possibility of a 'sudden fright' as the cause of death.
deductions.conclusion: Holmes concludes that a sudden fright is unlikely and there was probably a more tangible cause for Julia Stoner's death.

deductions.observation: her sister could smell Dr. Roylott's cigar
deductions.inference: that suggested at once that there must be a communication between the two rooms.

deductions.observation: communication between the two rooms
deductions.inference: It could only be a small one, or it would have been remarked upon at the coroner's inquiry.
deductions.conclusion: I deduced a ventilator.

deductions.observation: A ventilator is made, a cord is hung, and a lady who sleeps in the bed dies.
deductions.conclusion: curious coincidence of dates

deductions.observation: A ventilator is made, a cord is hung, and a lady who sleeps in the bed dies.
deductions.inference: There is a curious coincidence of dates between these events.
deductions.conclusion: These events are connected and suspicious, suggesting a planned crime.

deductions.observation: The bed was clamped to the floor.
deductions.inference: The lady could not move her bed.
deductions.conclusion: The bed must always be in the same relative position to the ventilator and to the rope.

deductions.observation: The cord was clearly never meant for a bell-pull.
deductions.inference: It is a rope with a different, sinister purpose.
deductions.conclusion: The rope is an integral part of the crime mechanism.

deductions.observation: The combination of the clamped bed, the ventilator, and the rope.
deductions.inference: These elements are designed to facilitate a subtle and horrible crime.
deductions.conclusion: They are only just in time to prevent some subtle and horrible crime.

deductions.observation: what seemed to be a hideous and distorted child, who threw itself upon the grass with writhing limbs and then ran swiftly across the lawn into the darkness.
deductions.inference: Based on the creature's appearance, behavior, and prior knowledge of Dr. Roylott's unusual pets.
deductions.conclusion: That is the baboon.

deductions.observation: The last echoes of a sound had died away into the silence.
deductions.inference: The sound indicated a decisive and final event had occurred.
deductions.conclusion: It means that it is all over.

deductions.observation: A peculiar yellow band, with brownish speckles, was bound tightly round Dr. Roylott's head.
deductions.inference: This is the 'speckled band' they were investigating.
deductions.conclusion: The band! the speckled band!

deductions.observation: The strange headgear began to move, and a squat diamond-shaped head and puffed neck of a loathsome serpent reared itself from among Dr. Roylott's hair.
deductions.inference: The 'speckled band' is a snake, specifically a swamp adder.
deductions.conclusion: It is a swamp adder! the deadliest snake in India.

deductions.observation: Dr. Roylott's rigid stare, the presence of the swamp adder, and the known deadliness of its bite.
deductions.inference: The swamp adder bit Dr. Roylott.
deductions.conclusion: He has died within ten seconds of being bitten.

deductions.observation: The presence of the gipsies.
deductions.inference: This observation, combined with the word 'band', led Holmes onto an entirely wrong scent.
deductions.conclusion: Holmes's initial conclusion about the case was entirely erroneous.

deductions.observation: The use of the word 'band' by the poor girl (Julia Stoner).
deductions.inference: This observation, combined with the presence of gipsies, led Holmes onto an entirely wrong scent.
deductions.conclusion: Holmes's initial conclusion about the case was entirely erroneous.

deductions.observation: whatever danger threatened an occupant of the room could not come either from the window or the door
deductions.inference: The danger must originate from an internal source within the room.

deductions.observation: My attention was speedily drawn... to this ventilator, and to the bell-rope which hung down to the bed.
this was a dummy (bell-rope)
the bed was clamped to the floor

deductions.inference: the rope was there as a bridge for something passing through the hole and coming to the bed.

deductions.conclusion: The idea of a snake instantly occurred to me

deductions.observation: my knowledge that the doctor was furnished with a supply of creatures from India
deductions.inference: The doctor has access to exotic and dangerous animals.

deductions.conclusion: I felt that I was probably on the right track (regarding the snake theory).

deductions.inference: The idea of using a form of poison which could not possibly be discovered by any chemical test was just such a one as would occur to a clever and ruthless man who had had an Eastern training.
The rapidity with which such a poison would take effect would also, from his point of view, be an advantage.

deductions.observation: the two little dark punctures which would show where the poison fangs had done their work
the whistle

deductions.inference: He must recall the snake before the morning light revealed it to the victim.
He had trained it, probably by the use of the milk which we saw, to return to him when summoned.
He would put it through this (ventilator/hole).

deductions.observation: An inspection of his chair showed me that he had been in the habit of standing on it
deductions.inference: which of course would be necessary in order that he should reach the ventilator.
deductions.conclusion: Dr. Grimesby Roylott used the chair to reach the ventilator.

deductions.observation: The sight of the safe, the saucer of milk, and the loop of whipcord
deductions.inference: These items confirmed the method of the crime involving the snake.
deductions.conclusion: All doubts about the snake's method were finally dispelled.

deductions.observation: The metallic clang heard by Miss Stoner
deductions.inference: was obviously caused by her stepfather hastily closing the door of his safe upon its terrible occupant.
deductions.conclusion: The metallic clang was Dr. Grimesby Roylott closing the safe with the snake inside.

scenes.title: Holmes's Deductions on the Crime Mechanism
scenes.description: As they travel back, Holmes explains to Watson how he initially reached an erroneous conclusion due to insufficient data, specifically regarding the gipsies and the 'band'. | Holmes explains his observations about the ventilator, cord, and clamped bed, leading Watson to understand the imminent danger. | Holmes, Watson, and Miss Stoner walk on the lawn after investigating Dr. Roylott's chamber. Holmes then outlines a detailed plan for Miss Stoner to follow, involving her room and a signal, to catch the culprit. | The narrator reflects on the numerous cases he has studied with Sherlock Holmes, noting their unusual nature and introducing the Roylott case as particularly singular.

scenes.title: Introduction to the Roylott Case
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson discuss the case, with Holmes stating his morning's work proved strong motives. Holmes instructs Watson to bring his revolver as they prepare to leave for Waterloo. | Holmes and Watson travel by cab to Waterloo, then by train to Leatherhead, and finally by trap through the Surrey lanes. Holmes is deep in thought during the journey. | The narrator introduces the case involving the Roylotts of Stoke Moran, mentioning it occurred early in his association with Holmes and that a promise of secrecy has only recently been lifted due to a lady's death. | Watson quickly dresses, eager to join Holmes in his professional investigations, as they prepare to go to the sitting-room.

scenes.title: Morning Awakening in Baker Street
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson wait in silence. A light and the smell of burning oil emanate from the ventilator. A gentle, hissing sound prompts Holmes to spring from bed, strike a match, and furiously lash at the bell-pull with his cane. Watson hears a whistle, and then a horrible cry breaks the silence. | The narrator describes waking up in April '83 to find Sherlock Holmes, fully dressed, by his bed in Baker Street. | While traveling through Surrey, Holmes suddenly points out a heavily timbered park stretching up a slope.

scenes.title: Morning Interruption in Watson's Bedroom
scenes.description: Watson is woken by Sherlock Holmes in his bedroom early in the morning, who explains that an urgent client has arrived.

scenes.title: Holmes Investigates the Will and Uncovers Financial Motive
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson enter the Manor House grounds through a breach in the wall, cross the lawn, and encounter a baboon. | Holmes and Watson enter the bedroom, close the shutters, and Holmes moves the lamp. | Holmes and Watson enter the sitting-room and are met by a young lady, heavily veiled and dressed in black, who rises upon their entrance. | Holmes and Watson leave the house, speak to the landlord, and proceed along a dark road towards the grounds. | Holmes and Watson meet a heavily veiled lady in their sitting-room. She expresses extreme fear and agitation, prompting Holmes to offer comfort and begin his observations. | Holmes and the narrator discuss their plan to spend the night in Miss Stoner's room to investigate the disturbing noise, and Holmes reassures her about the dangers, while Miss Stoner presses him for his current thoughts on her sister's death. | Holmes visits Doctors' Commons to examine the will of the deceased wife. Upon his return, he explains to Watson the financial implications of the will, revealing that the marriage of the daughters would severely diminish Dr. Roylott's income, thus establishing a strong motive for the crimes.

scenes.title: Holmes Explains the Snake's Mechanism and Roylott's Death
scenes.description: A distressed lady arrives, and Holmes immediately deduces details about her journey from mud on her jacket. She confirms his deduction and explains her predicament, mentioning Mrs. Farintosh as a reference. Holmes consults his case-book and agrees to take her case. | At eleven o'clock, a bright light shines from the Manor House, signaling Holmes and Watson to proceed. Holmes briefly speaks with the landlord before they leave. | Dr. Grimesby Roylott bursts into Holmes's rooms, demanding to know what his stepdaughter, Miss Stoner, has told Holmes. He displays extreme anger and threatens Holmes, demonstrating his dangerous character by bending a steel poker. | Dr. Roylott confronts Holmes and Watson, demonstrating his physical strength and aggressive nature by bending a poker and issuing a threat before leaving. Holmes then demonstrates his own comparable strength. | Helen Stoner describes the terrifying death of her sister, Julia, who screams about 'the speckled band' before collapsing and dying, despite attempts to revive her. | Helen Stoner visits Holmes and Watson to describe her vague fears and suspicions regarding her dangerous situation, and Holmes acknowledges the historical background of the Roylott family. | Holmes and Miss Stoner discuss Dr. Roylott's pursuit. Miss Stoner expresses her fear, and Holmes advises her to lock herself in and plans to examine the rooms. | Holmes and Watson discover Dr. Roylott dead from a snake bite, identify the 'swamp adder' as the cause, secure the snake, and arrange for Miss Stoner's safety and police notification. | Holmes and Watson hear a dreadful sound from Dr. Roylott's room. Holmes declares 'it is all over' and decides they must enter the room, taking a pistol. | Holmes explains his deductions regarding Dr. Grimesby Roylott's method of using the snake, the objects involved (chair, safe, milk, whipcord), and how his intervention led to the snake turning on and killing Roylott. | Holmes questions the client, observes marks of abuse on her wrist, and decides to visit Stoke Moran to investigate further. | The client describes hearing the ominous whistle again during the night, prompting her to leave her home and travel to Holmes for help.

scenes.title: Dr. Roylott's Decline at Stoke Moran
scenes.description: After the mother's death, Dr. Roylott abandons his London practice and moves to Stoke Moran, where he undergoes a terrible change, becoming violent and reclusive, terrorizing the local village.

scenes.title: Helen Stoner recounts Dr. Roylott's behavior and Julia's death
scenes.description: Helen Stoner describes her stepfather's eccentric and intimidating behavior, his association with gipsies and dangerous Indian animals, and then recounts the circumstances leading up to her sister Julia's death two years prior, including Julia's engagement and the sudden 'terrible event'. Sherlock Holmes listens intently.

scenes.title: Helen Stoner recounts Julia's last night
scenes.description: Helen Stoner, the client, recounts to Sherlock Holmes the details of her sister Julia's last night, including her concerns about a mysterious whistle.

scenes.title: Helen recounts the mysterious whistle and locked doors
scenes.description: La narradora le pregunta a Holmes sobre un silbido que ha escuchado por las noches y discute la costumbre de cerrar las puertas con llave debido a los animales del Doctor.

scenes.title: The night of Julia's death
scenes.description: La narradora describe la noche en que su hermana Julia murió, escuchando un grito aterrador y un silbido mientras corría hacia el pasillo.

scenes.title: Planning the visit to Stoke Moran and initial reflections
scenes.description: Holmes, Watson, and the client discuss the possibility of visiting Stoke Moran without the stepfather's knowledge. The client departs, and Holmes and Watson begin to reflect on the contradictory evidence.

scenes.title: Holmes's Theory and Decision to Visit Stoke Moran
scenes.description: Holmes discusses his developing theory about the mystery, combining various observations, and decides to visit Stoke Moran with Watson to test his hypothesis.

scenes.title: Interruption by a Mysterious Man
scenes.description: As Holmes and Watson discuss, their door is suddenly dashed open, and a huge, imposing man appears in the doorway, interrupting their conversation.

scenes.title: Arrival and identification of Stoke Moran
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson arrive near Stoke Moran, identify the mansion, and observe building work.

scenes.title: Approach to Stoke Moran and meeting Miss Stoner
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson leave the trap, pay the driver, and take a footpath to meet Miss Stoner.

scenes.title: Miss Stoner's update on Dr. Roylott's absence
scenes.description: Miss Stoner greets Holmes and Watson, informing them that Dr. Roylott has gone to town, and reacts strongly to Holmes's account of meeting him.

scenes.title: Examination of Stoke Moran Exterior
scenes.description: Holmes and Miss Stoner examine the exterior of the Stoke Moran building, noting its dilapidated state and identifying the residents' rooms.

scenes.title: Exterior Examination of the Rooms
scenes.description: Holmes and Miss Stoner examine the exterior of the rooms, focusing on the windows and shutters, and Holmes attempts to force a shutter open to test its security. | Holmes and Miss Stoner move inside to examine the corridor and the bedrooms, particularly the second chamber where Julia Stoner died and Miss Stoner is now sleeping.

scenes.title: Examination of Miss Stoner's Chamber
scenes.description: Holmes and Miss Stoner are in the second chamber, where Julia Stoner died. Holmes meticulously examines the room, focusing on a bell-rope and the floorboards, questioning Miss Stoner about the bell-rope's purpose and history. | Holmes minutely examines the floor, woodwork, bed, and discovers the dummy bell-rope and non-ventilating ventilator in Miss Stoner's chamber.

scenes.title: Entry into Dr. Roylott's Chamber
scenes.description: Holmes and Miss Stoner move into Dr. Grimesby Roylott's chamber, which is described as larger and plainly furnished, containing a camp-bed, shelf of books, armchair, wooden chair, round table, and a large iron safe.

scenes.title: Holmes examines Dr. Roylott's chamber
scenes.description: Holmes meticulously inspects the contents of Dr. Roylott's chamber, discovering a saucer of milk and a peculiar tied dog lash, while questioning Miss Stoner.

scenes.title: Observation from the Crown Inn
scenes.description: Sherlock Holmes and the narrator secure a room at the Crown Inn, overlooking Stoke Moran Manor House, and observe Dr. Roylott's arrival, noting his aggressive behavior towards the lad driving him.

scenes.title: Holmes and Watson discuss danger and initial deductions
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson sit together in the gathering darkness, discussing the inherent danger of the investigation and Holmes's initial deductions regarding the ventilator and bell-rope, based on Miss Stoner's statement about her sister smelling Dr. Roylott's cigar.

scenes.title: Waiting for the Signal
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson wait in the dark near the Manor House after the lights are extinguished, discussing the dangerous nature of criminal doctors.

scenes.title: Vigil in the dark room
scenes.description: Holmes and the narrator sit in absolute darkness, waiting silently. Holmes gives instructions to the narrator, emphasizing the danger and the need for vigilance. They hear a catlike whine outside and the parish clock striking, before a momentary gleam of light appears near the ventilator.

scenes.title: Discovery of Dr. Roylott's Body and the Snake
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson enter Dr. Roylott's room, finding him dead in a chair with a dark-lantern and safe nearby. They discover a peculiar speckled band on his head, which reveals itself to be a venomous serpent, a swamp adder.
