deductions.observation: For years past I have continually been conscious of some power behind the malefactor, some deep organizing power which forever stands in the way of the law, and throws its shield over the wrong-doer.
deductions.inference: Again and again in cases of the most varying sorts—forgery cases, robberies, murders—I have felt the presence of this force, and I have deduced its action in many of those undiscovered crimes in which I have not been personally consulted.
deductions.conclusion: This power is ex-Professor Moriarty of mathematical celebrity, the organizer of half that is evil and of nearly all that is undetected in this great city.

deductions.observation: Holmes's frontal development
deductions.conclusion: Holmes has less frontal development than Moriarty expected.

deductions.observation: Holmes is fingering something in the pocket of his dressing-gown.
deductions.inference: The object Holmes is fingering is a loaded firearm.
deductions.conclusion: It is a dangerous habit to finger loaded firearms in the pocket of one's dressing-gown.

deductions.observation: A brick came down from the roof of one of the houses, and was shattered to fragments at my feet.
deductions.inference: The falling brick was not an accident caused by the wind.
deductions.conclusion: The falling brick was a deliberate attempt on my life.

deductions.observation: There were slates and bricks piled up on the roof preparatory to some repairs, and they would have me believe that the wind had toppled over one of these.
deductions.inference: The official explanation of the falling brick being caused by wind is false.
deductions.conclusion: The incident was orchestrated, not accidental.

deductions.observation: I was attacked by a rough with a bludgeon.
deductions.inference: The attacker is a mere pawn, not the mastermind.
deductions.conclusion: No possible connection will ever be traced between the attacker and Professor Moriarty.

deductions.observation: Moriarty is seen pushing his way furiously through the crowd and waving his hand as if he desired to have the train stopped.
deductions.inference: Moriarty is attempting to stop the train.
deductions.conclusion: Moriarty is 'hot upon our trail' and has located them.

deductions.observation: The train had already begun to move and was rapidly gathering momentum, shooting clear of the station.
deductions.inference: Moriarty's attempt to stop the train is too late.
deductions.conclusion: They 'have cut it rather fine' in their escape.

deductions.observation: Their 'bludgeon-man was arrested'.
deductions.inference: The enemy must have lost Holmes's track completely after the arrest.
deductions.conclusion: They could not have imagined Holmes was still in London, leading to the arson at Baker Street.

deductions.observation: They set fire to our rooms last night.
deductions.inference: They must have lost my track completely after their bludgeon-man was arrested. Otherwise they could not have imagined that I had returned to my rooms. They have evidently taken the precaution of watching you, however, and that is what has brought Moriarty to Victoria.
deductions.conclusion: Moriarty is pursuing us and has arrived at Victoria by watching Watson.

deductions.observation: Watson did not recognise his coachman.
deductions.conclusion: It was my brother Mycroft.

deductions.observation: This train stops at Canterbury; and there is always at least a quarter of an hour's delay at the boat.
deductions.inference: Moriarty is on the same intellectual plane as myself and would anticipate this opportunity.
deductions.conclusion: He will catch us there.

deductions.observation: Far away, from among the Kentish woods there rose a thin spray of smoke. A minute later a carriage and engine could be seen flying along the open curve which leads to the station.
deductions.inference: The approaching train is carrying Moriarty, who is pursuing them.
deductions.conclusion: Moriarty is following their original expected route.

deductions.observation: Moriarty's train passes through Canterbury, indicating he is following the original route to Paris.
deductions.inference: Moriarty failed to deduce Holmes's counter-move of alighting at Canterbury and changing routes.
deductions.conclusion: There are limits to Moriarty's intelligence, as he did not anticipate Holmes's strategy.

deductions.observation: Moriarty will get on to Paris, mark down our luggage, and wait for two days at the depôt.
deductions.inference: Moriarty will mimic Holmes's expected actions, assuming Holmes would continue to Paris with his luggage.
deductions.conclusion: Moriarty will be misled by their change of plans and waste time in Paris.

deductions.observation: Moriarty did not overtake Holmes and Watson.
deductions.inference: He deduced what I would deduce and acted accordingly.
deductions.conclusion: Moriarty is highly intelligent and anticipates Holmes's moves.

deductions.observation: The telegram states that Moriarty has escaped.
deductions.inference: When I had left the country there was no one to cope with him.
deductions.conclusion: Moriarty gave the police the slip.

deductions.observation: Moriarty's occupation is gone, and he is lost if he returns to London.
deductions.inference: If I read his character right he will devote his whole energies to revenging himself upon me.
deductions.conclusion: Watson will find me a dangerous companion now, and should return to his practice.

deductions.observation: A large rock was dislodged from the ridge upon our right clattered down and roared into the lake behind us.
deductions.inference: Holmes suspects the rockfall was not a natural occurrence but an intentional act.
deductions.conclusion: The danger (Moriarty's agents) is still pursuing them and attempting to harm him.

deductions.observation: It was the sight of that Alpine-stock
deductions.inference: He had not gone to Rosenlaui, then.
deductions.conclusion: Holmes had remained on that three-foot path.

deductions.observation: The young Swiss had gone too.
deductions.inference: He had probably been in the pay of Moriarty, and had left the two men together.

deductions.observation: Two lines of footmarks were clearly marked along the farther end of the path, both leading away from me. There were none returning.
deductions.inference: Two individuals proceeded along the path, and neither came back.

deductions.observation: A few yards from the end the soil was all ploughed up into a patch of mud, and the branches and ferns which fringed the chasm were torn and bedraggled.
deductions.inference: A violent struggle or disturbance occurred at that specific point.

deductions.observation: The combined physical evidence at the scene (Alpine-stock location, missing Swiss, footmarks, disturbed soil and vegetation).
deductions.inference: Holmes and his enemy engaged in a struggle.
deductions.conclusion: Both Holmes and his enemy fell into the chasm.

deductions.observation: From the top of this boulder the gleam of something bright caught my eye
deductions.inference: The bright gleam indicates an object of significance left behind.
deductions.conclusion: There is an object on the boulder that warrants investigation.

deductions.observation: I found that it came from the silver cigarette-case which he used to carry
deductions.inference: The cigarette-case belongs to Holmes.
deductions.conclusion: The bright object is Holmes's silver cigarette-case.

deductions.observation: a small square of paper upon which it had lain fluttered down on to the ground
deductions.inference: The paper was intentionally placed with the cigarette-case.
deductions.conclusion: The paper is a message or item left by Holmes.

deductions.observation: it consisted of three pages torn from his note-book and addressed to me
deductions.inference: The note is a personal communication from Holmes to Watson.
deductions.conclusion: Holmes left a detailed message for Watson.

deductions.observation: the direction was a precise, and the writing as firm and clear, as though it had been written in his study
deductions.inference: Holmes maintained composure and clarity of thought while writing the note.
deductions.conclusion: Holmes was calm and deliberate despite the impending confrontation.

deductions.observation: I was quite convinced that the letter from Meiringen was a hoax
deductions.inference: The content or circumstances of the letter indicated deception.
deductions.conclusion: The letter that lured Watson away was a trick.

scenes.title: Narrator's Reflection on Holmes's Recent Activities
scenes.description: Holmes describes a brick falling from a roof and shattering at his feet while walking down Vere Street, which he believes was a deliberate attack despite police attributing it to wind. | Holmes recounts being nearly run over by a two-horse van while transacting business in Oxford Street, near Bentinck Street and Welbeck Street crossing. | The narrator reflects on the period after his marriage, the modification of his relationship with Holmes, and Holmes's engagement by the French government, including receiving notes from Narbonne and Nimes.

scenes.title: Holmes's Unexpected Arrival and Request for Privacy
scenes.description: Holmes explains to Watson the extreme danger he is in from Moriarty's syndicate, justifying his need for secrecy and an inconspicuous exit. He then invites Watson to accompany him to the Continent and provides detailed instructions for their departure the following morning. | Holmes unexpectedly arrives at the narrator's consulting-room on the evening of April 24th, looking pale and thin. He immediately asks to close and then securely bolts the shutters.

scenes.title: Holmes Reveals Moriarty's Background and His Discovery
scenes.description: After the second attack, Holmes takes a cab to his brother's rooms in Pall Mall and spends the day there. | Holmes and Watson discuss Moriarty's intelligence and his anticipated actions, including a potential murderous attack, while considering their next meal. | Holmes and Watson discuss their escape plan by train, with Holmes revealing Mycroft's involvement and emphasizing Moriarty's intellectual prowess and relentless pursuit, predicting he will catch them at Canterbury. | Holmes arrives at Watson's rooms, immediately closes the shutters, and requests to leave by a less conspicuous exit, indicating his heightened state of alert. | Holmes explains to Watson the background of ex-Professor Moriarty, his hereditary criminal tendencies, and how Holmes himself, through years of observation and deduction, uncovered Moriarty as the hidden mastermind behind London's criminal underworld. | Holmes informs Watson about the arson attempt on their rooms and deduces Moriarty's movements, revealing that Moriarty is pursuing them to Victoria. | Holmes, concerned about Moriarty's impending revenge, advises Watson to return to England for his safety, leading to an argument in a Strasburg _salle-à-manger_. | Holmes, concerned about bringing trouble to his current lodging, leaves immediately by clambering over a wall into Mortimer Street and whistling for a hansom. | In Strasburg, Holmes receives a telegram from the London police, confirming that Moriarty has escaped, leading to Holmes's bitter frustration. | Sherlock Holmes makes a late-night, urgent visit to Dr. Watson's house, bolting the shutters and expressing fear of 'air-guns.' He reveals his injured knuckles, indicating a recent struggle, and proposes that Watson accompany him on an immediate, indefinite trip to the Continent, hinting at grave danger. | The narrator reaches Reichenbach Falls, finds Holmes's Alpine-stock but no sign of Holmes, and realizes he has been attacked. | Watson is startled by Holmes, disguised as an aged ecclesiastic, on a moving train. Holmes reveals the need for precautions as Moriarty appears at the station, attempting to stop the train. | Watson narrates the presumed deaths of Sherlock Holmes and Professor Moriarty in a struggle at Reichenbach Falls, their bodies lost in the caldron. The disappearance of a Swiss youth, an agent of Moriarty, is noted, along with the subsequent exposure of Moriarty's gang due to Holmes's accumulated evidence. | Watson waits anxiously for Holmes at Victoria Station, noting the time and searching for his friend, and briefly assists an Italian priest. | While at the Reichenbach Falls, a Swiss lad delivers a letter to the narrator from the landlord of the hotel they just left, reporting the arrival of an English lady in poor health.

scenes.title: Holmes Introduces Professor Moriarty
scenes.description: Holmes, appearing pale and worn, explains to Watson the existence and dangerous nature of Professor Moriarty, a criminal mastermind operating unseen in London. He reflects on his past cases for the royal family of Scandinavia and the French republic, and expresses his ultimate goal of bringing Moriarty down. | The next morning, Watson procures a hansom with precautions, drives to the Lowther Arcade, dashes through it, and steps into a waiting brougham which then takes him to Victoria. | While Holmes is reflecting in his room, Professor Moriarty unexpectedly appears, confronting Holmes directly.

scenes.title: Holmes explains Moriarty's criminal organization and impending capture
scenes.description: Holmes describes Professor Moriarty as the 'Napoleon of crime' and the mastermind behind a vast criminal network. He explains his long struggle to gather evidence against Moriarty, how Moriarty made a crucial mistake ('a trip'), and how Holmes has now woven a net around him, expecting to capture Moriarty and his gang in three days.

scenes.title: Holmes's Third Attack En Route to Watson's
scenes.description: Despite Holmes's advice, Watson remains with him, and they resume their journey, heading towards Geneva. | Holmes explains his elaborate plan to capture Professor Moriarty and his entire gang within three days, leading to a major criminal trial. | Holmes gives detailed instructions to Watson for their coordinated escape the next morning, involving specific hansom and brougham arrangements to reach Victoria for the Continental express. | On May 4th, advised by Peter Steiler the elder, Holmes and Watson set off to cross the hills with the intention of spending the night at the hamlet of Rosenlaui. | On his way to Watson's rooms, Holmes is attacked by a rough with a bludgeon, whom he knocks down and the police take into custody. | Sherlock Holmes writes a letter to Watson from Meiringen, confessing his understanding of the situation with Moriarty, giving instructions for Inspector Patterson regarding the gang, and mentioning the disposition of his property to Mycroft, before bidding farewell. | The narrator and his companion depart from the Grosvenor Hotel in London, intending to cross the hills and spend the night at Rosenlaui, making a detour to see the Reichenbach Falls. | The narrator walks along a curving path towards Meiringen, observing a rapidly walking man. | The narrator, filled with fear, rushes back down the village street towards Reichenbach Falls. | Watson hurries through Lowther Arcade and is driven by a massive driver in a brougham to Victoria Station.

scenes.title: Moriarty's Confrontation with Holmes
scenes.description: Holmes and Professor Moriarty have a tense conversation where Moriarty issues direct threats against Holmes. | Professor Moriarty visits Holmes, observing his physical traits and deducing the presence of a hidden firearm. A tense verbal exchange ensues, culminating in Moriarty revealing he has been tracking Holmes's interference with his criminal operations.

scenes.title: Confrontation and Warning
scenes.description: The Professor confronts Mr. Holmes, detailing how Holmes has hampered his criminal plans since January and warns him to withdraw, threatening 'inevitable destruction' if he continues. Holmes refuses to back down.

scenes.title: Holmes's outing to Oxford Street
scenes.description: Holmes leaves his residence to conduct business in Oxford Street, where an implied assault has occurred or is expected.

scenes.title: Holmes's Appearance in the Carriage
scenes.description: As the train is about to depart, Holmes unexpectedly reveals himself inside Watson's carriage, having been there all along.

scenes.title: Revelation of Baker Street Arson
scenes.description: Holmes sheds his disguise and informs Watson that their rooms at Baker Street were set on fire the previous night, implying it was a consequence of the 'bludgeon-man's' arrest.

scenes.title: Holmes outlines the escape plan
scenes.description: Holmes explains to Watson their strategy to evade Moriarty, involving a cross-country journey to Newhaven and then to Dieppe, while Moriarty is expected to go to Paris.

scenes.title: Moriarty's pursuit at Canterbury
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson alight at Canterbury and observe Moriarty's train passing through, confirming his pursuit and his failure to anticipate their change of plans.

scenes.title: Journey to Brussels and Strasburg
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson travel from their previous location to Brussels, spend two days there, and then continue their journey to Strasburg.

scenes.title: Argument in Strasburg
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson argue in a salle-à-manger in Strasburg about continuing their journey, with Watson eventually conceding. | Holmes and Watson arrive in the village of Meiringen on May 3rd and take lodging at the Englischer Hof, run by Peter Steiler the elder.

scenes.title: Journey through the Alps
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson travel through the Valley of the Rhone, Leuk, over the snowy Gemmi Pass, and via Interlaken to Meiringen, with Holmes remaining vigilant throughout the trip.

scenes.title: The Rockfall on Gemmi Pass
scenes.description: While crossing the Gemmi Pass near the Daubensee, a large rock falls from a ridge. Holmes immediately investigates, suspecting foul play despite the guide's assurances.

scenes.title: Holmes's Reflection on his Career
scenes.description: Holmes expresses his satisfaction with his career, his belief that he has not lived in vain, and his ultimate goal of capturing or eliminating Professor Moriarty.

scenes.title: Watson is persuaded to return to Meiringen
scenes.description: Watson is convinced by the landlord, Steiler, to return to Meiringen under the pretense of attending to a dying English lady, leaving Holmes alone.

scenes.title: Watson leaves Holmes at the fall
scenes.description: Watson departs from Holmes, who remains at the fall, and begins his descent towards Meiringen.

scenes.title: Watson observes a man approaching Holmes
scenes.description: As Watson descends, he looks back and sees a rapidly walking black-figured man on the path leading to the fall, heading towards Holmes's position.

scenes.title: Discovery of the Trick Letter
scenes.description: The narrator arrives at Meiringen, speaks with Steiler, and realizes the letter about a sick Englishwoman is a ruse.

scenes.title: Watson Investigates the Reichenbach Falls Path
scenes.description: Watson returns to the path near the Reichenbach Falls, finds Holmes's Alpine-stock, and examines the ground for clues, deducing what happened to Holmes and Moriarty.

scenes.title: Watson discovers Holmes's farewell note
scenes.description: Watson finds Holmes's silver cigarette-case and a note on a boulder near the path, where Holmes had left his Alpine-stock. The note, written by Holmes, explains his impending final confrontation with Mr. Moriarty and reveals his conviction that the letter from Meiringen was a hoax.

events.name: First meeting of Holmes and Watson
events.description: The initial encounter between Mr. Sherlock Holmes and the narrator, which occurred during the period of 'A Study in Scarlet'.

events.name: Holmes's interference in the Naval Treaty case
events.description: Mr. Sherlock Holmes's intervention in the matter of the 'Naval Treaty', which had the unquestionable effect of preventing a serious international complication.

events.name: The event creating a void in the narrator's life
events.description: An unspecified event that has created a void in the narrator's life, which two years have done little to fill.

events.name: Colonel Moriarty's letters
events.description: Recent letters written by Colonel James Moriarty defending the memory of his brother, which compelled the narrator to reveal the facts.

events.name: Public press accounts
events.description: Three accounts published in the public press: in the Journal de Genève on May 6th, 1891, Reuter's despatch in English papers on May 7th, and a recent letter.

events.name: Holmes engaged by French government
events.description: Holmes was engaged by the French government on a matter of supreme importance during the winter of 1890 and early spring of 1891.

events.name: Holmes's unexpected visit to consulting-room
events.description: Holmes unexpectedly arrived at the narrator's consulting-room on the evening of April 24th, looking pale and thin.

events.name: Holmes secures the shutters
events.description: Holmes closed and bolted the shutters in the narrator's consulting-room, indicating a need for privacy or security.

events.name: Holmes's late-night visit to Watson
events.description: Holmes arrives at Watson's house late at night, exhibiting unusual behavior and urgency.

events.name: Holmes expresses fear of air-guns
events.description: Holmes bolts the shutters and admits to Watson that he is afraid of air-guns, indicating a specific threat.

events.name: Holmes reveals injured knuckles
events.description: Holmes shows Watson his burst and bleeding knuckles, suggesting a recent physical confrontation.

events.name: Holmes proposes a trip to the Continent
events.description: Holmes asks Watson to accompany him on an immediate trip to the Continent for a week, without specifying a destination.

events.name: Holmes reveals Professor Moriarty's existence
events.description: Holmes informs Watson about Professor Moriarty, describing him as a brilliant but diabolical criminal mastermind whose defeat would be the summit of Holmes's career.

events.name: Holmes Gives Departure Instructions to Watson
events.description: After an argument, Holmes and Watson resume their journey towards Geneva from Strasburg. | Due to dark rumours in the university town, ex-Professor Moriarty was compelled to resign his mathematical chair and move to London, where he set up as an Army coach. | Holmes and Watson continue their journey towards Geneva, despite Holmes's concerns for Watson's safety. | Holmes provides Watson with specific instructions for dispatching luggage and taking a hansom cab the next morning to avoid detection. | Mr. Holmes refuses the Professor's demand to withdraw from the investigation, stating 'Danger is part of my trade' and that he will continue after Monday. | The Professor warns Mr. Holmes to cease his interference, stating that Holmes has hampered his plans and is now in danger of losing his liberty, threatening 'inevitable destruction' if he does not withdraw.

events.name: Holmes's Discovery of Moriarty
events.description: After years of being conscious of a hidden organizing power behind various crimes, Holmes followed a 'thread' that led him to identify ex-Professor Moriarty as the 'Napoleon of crime'. | Moriarty's men set fire to Holmes's rooms at Baker Street, believing Holmes had returned. | The evidence gathered by Sherlock Holmes leads to the complete exposure and downfall of Moriarty's criminal organization.

events.name: Moriarty makes a crucial mistake
events.description: Professor Moriarty made a 'little, little trip' which allowed Holmes to gain an advantage in his pursuit.

events.name: Holmes's net is ready to close
events.description: Holmes has successfully woven a 'net' around Professor Moriarty and his organization, and it is now ready to close.

events.name: Impending arrest of Moriarty and his gang
events.description: Holmes reveals that in three days (on Monday next), Professor Moriarty and all the principal members of his gang will be arrested by the police.

events.name: Holmes's plan to capture Moriarty's gang
events.description: Holmes details his strategy to ensnare Professor Moriarty and his principal gang members, expecting their arrest in three days.

events.name: Professor Moriarty confronts Holmes
events.description: Professor Moriarty makes an unannounced appearance in Holmes's room, surprising Holmes.

events.name: Professor Moriarty's visit to Holmes
events.description: Professor Moriarty arrives at Holmes's residence for a direct confrontation.

events.name: Moriarty deduces Holmes's hidden firearm
events.description: Professor Moriarty observes Holmes's actions and deduces that Holmes has a loaded firearm concealed in his dressing-gown pocket.

events.name: Holmes draws his weapon
events.description: In response to Moriarty's remark, Holmes draws his revolver and places it cocked on the table.

events.name: Moriarty reveals tracking dates
events.description: Professor Moriarty produces a memorandum-book containing dates, indicating he has been meticulously tracking Holmes's interference with his criminal activities.

events.name: Interview between Holmes and Moriarty
events.description: A direct confrontation where Professor Moriarty threatens Holmes's life and career, stating he will bring destruction upon him.

events.name: Moriarty's threats to Holmes
events.description: Professor Moriarty explicitly threatens Holmes, stating that if Holmes attempts to bring him to justice, Moriarty will retaliate with destruction.

events.name: Holmes goes to Oxford Street
events.description: Holmes leaves his residence about midday to transact some business in Oxford Street.

events.name: Implied assault on Holmes
events.description: Watson asks Holmes if he has been assaulted, and Holmes confirms he expects a 'blow' from Moriarty's agents, implying a recent or imminent attack.

events.name: Rockfall Incident on Gemmi Pass
events.description: A brick falls from a roof in Vere Street, narrowly missing Holmes, which he identifies as a deliberate attack. | A large rock falls from a ridge on the Gemmi Pass, which Holmes perceives as a deliberate attempt on his life. | Holmes is attacked by a man with a bludgeon on his way to Watson's rooms, but he subdues the assailant. | Holmes is nearly run over by a two-horse van in Oxford Street, an attempt on his life.

events.name: Holmes takes refuge at brother's rooms
events.description: Following two attempts on his life, Holmes spends the day at his brother's rooms in Pall Mall for safety.

events.name: Holmes arrives at Watson's rooms and takes precautions
events.description: Holmes arrives at Watson's, immediately closes the shutters, and plans a discreet exit, indicating his awareness of ongoing danger.

events.name: Holmes Explains Precautions
events.description: Holmes and Watson undertake a week-long journey through the Alps, passing through the Rhone Valley, Leuk, Gemmi Pass, Interlaken, and Meiringen. | Holmes explains to Watson why he closed the shutters and needs to leave by an inconspicuous exit, due to the danger posed by Moriarty's syndicate.

events.name: Holmes Invites Watson to the Continent
events.description: Holmes asks Watson to accompany him to the Continent to escape the police and Moriarty's syndicate.

events.name: Holmes instructs Watson on escape plan
events.description: Holmes provides detailed instructions to Watson for their coordinated departure to avoid pursuit.

events.name: Holmes departs from his lodging
events.description: Holmes leaves his current lodging to avoid bringing trouble to his hosts, using a hansom from Mortimer Street.

events.name: Watson executes his part of the escape plan
events.description: Watson follows Holmes's instructions precisely, using specific transport arrangements to reach Victoria station.

events.name: Watson travels to Victoria Station
events.description: Watson takes a brougham from Lowther Arcade to Victoria Station.

events.name: Watson waits for Holmes
events.description: Watson anxiously waits for Holmes at Victoria Station as the departure time approaches.

events.name: Holmes appears in Watson's carriage
events.description: Holmes surprises Watson by revealing himself inside Watson's train carriage just as the train is about to leave.

events.name: Holmes reveals his disguise
events.description: Holmes, disguised as an aged ecclesiastic, reveals his true identity to Watson on the train.

events.name: Moriarty attempts to stop the train
events.description: Professor Moriarty is seen at the station, attempting to stop the train carrying Holmes and Watson.

events.name: The Final Struggle at Reichenbach Falls
events.description: Holmes and Watson reach the village of Meiringen on May 3rd and check into the Englischer Hof. | Holmes reveals that their rooms at Baker Street were set on fire the previous night. | Sherlock Holmes and Professor Moriarty engage in a personal contest at Reichenbach Falls, which results in both falling into the water and their bodies being unrecoverable.

events.name: Arrest of the bludgeon-man
events.description: A man involved in a previous attack on Holmes was arrested, leading to the enemy losing Holmes's track.

events.name: Mycroft acts as Watson's coachman
events.description: Mycroft Holmes disguises himself as Watson's coachman to ensure a secure journey for Watson to meet Sherlock.

events.name: Moriarty's pursuit to Canterbury
events.description: Holmes deduces that Moriarty will catch them at Canterbury due to the train's schedule and boat connection, highlighting Moriarty's relentless pursuit.

events.name: Holmes outlines escape plan
events.description: Holmes details their plan to travel to Newhaven, then Dieppe, and eventually Switzerland, to evade Moriarty who is expected to go to Paris.

events.name: Moriarty's train passes Canterbury
events.description: Holmes and Watson witness Moriarty's train passing through Canterbury, confirming his pursuit and his miscalculation of their route.

events.name: Moriarty's escape
events.description: Professor Moriarty escapes from the London police, while the rest of his gang is secured.

events.name: Holmes advises Watson to return to England
events.description: Fearing Moriarty's revenge, Holmes urges Watson to leave him and return to his medical practice for safety.

events.name: Holmes's contemplation of his career
events.description: Holmes reflects on his past achievements, his impact on society, and his ultimate mission to deal with Professor Moriarty.

events.name: Departure for Rosenlaui
events.description: On May 4th, Holmes and Watson begin their journey from Meiringen, intending to cross the hills and stay at Rosenlaui. | The narrator and his companion depart from the Grosvenor Hotel on the afternoon of the 4th, heading towards Rosenlaui, with a planned detour to Reichenbach Falls.

events.name: Receipt of the letter at Reichenbach Falls
events.description: A Swiss lad delivers a letter to the narrator at Reichenbach Falls, informing him of an urgent matter back at the hotel.

events.name: English lady's arrival at the hotel
events.description: An English lady, in the last stage of consumption, arrives at the Grosvenor Hotel shortly after the narrator and his companion depart, interrupting her journey from Davos Platz to Lucerne.

events.name: Watson's return to Meiringen
events.description: Watson is convinced by Steiler to return to Meiringen to attend to a supposedly dying English lady, leaving Holmes alone at the fall.

events.name: Observation of a mysterious figure
events.description: Watson observes a man walking rapidly along the path towards Holmes's location at the fall after Watson has started his descent.

events.name: Narrator receives a fake letter
events.description: The narrator receives a letter supposedly from Steiler, asking him to come to Meiringen due to a sick Englishwoman, which turns out to be a ruse.

events.name: Holmes disappears at Reichenbach Falls
events.description: The narrator returns to Reichenbach Falls to find Holmes's Alpine-stock but no sign of Holmes, leading to the realization that he has been attacked.

events.name: Apparent Fall of Holmes and Moriarty
events.description: Holmes and Moriarty apparently struggled at the edge of the path and fell into the chasm, as deduced by Watson from the physical evidence.

events.name: Watson discovers Holmes's note
events.description: Watson finds Holmes's silver cigarette-case containing a farewell note on a boulder.

events.name: Holmes's final message to Watson
events.description: Holmes's note explains his confrontation with Moriarty and his belief that the Meiringen letter was a hoax.

events.name: Holmes's confrontation with Moriarty
events.description: Holmes indicates he is about to have a 'final discussion' with Mr. Moriarty.

events.name: Meiringen letter revealed as a hoax
events.description: Holmes states his conviction that the letter from Meiringen, which led Watson away, was a hoax.

events.name: Holmes's Confession and Instructions
events.description: Sherlock Holmes confesses to Watson that he knew the letter from Meiringen was a hoax and anticipated a confrontation with Moriarty. He instructs Watson to tell Inspector Patterson about the papers to convict the gang and mentions entrusting his property to Mycroft.

events.name: Disappearance of the Swiss Youth
events.description: A Swiss youth, believed to be one of Moriarty's agents, is never found after the incident at Reichenbach Falls.

deductions.inference: You told me, four weeks ago, that Thurston had an option on some South African property which would expire in a month, and which he desired you to share with him.

deductions.observation: Watson's check book is locked in Holmes's drawer, and Watson has not asked for the key.
deductions.conclusion: You do not propose to invest your money in this manner.

deductions.observation: groove between Watson's left forefinger and thumb, combined with knowledge of his habits and Thurston's business
deductions.inference: Watson has been playing billiards with Thurston, who has an expiring option on South African property he wants Watson to share.
deductions.conclusion: You did not propose to invest your small capital in the gold fields.

deductions.observation: It is certainly rather a curious production.
deductions.inference: At first sight it would appear to be some childish prank.

deductions.observation: It consists of a number of absurd little figures dancing across the paper upon which they are drawn.
It was a page torn from a notebook. The markings were done in pencil, and ran in this way: AM-HERE-ABE-SLANEY
These hieroglyphics have evidently a meaning.
deductions.inference: The meaning could be either purely arbitrary or systematic.
deductions.conclusion: If purely arbitrary, it may be impossible to solve; if systematic, it can be solved.

deductions.observation: This particular sample is so short and the facts brought are so indefinite.
deductions.conclusion: I can do nothing, and we have no basis for an investigation yet.

deductions.observation: this particular sample is so short
deductions.conclusion: I can do nothing

deductions.observation: the facts which you have brought me are so indefinite
deductions.conclusion: we have no basis for an investigation

deductions.observation: a wire from Hilton Cubitt this morning
deductions.inference: He was to reach Liverpool Street at one-twenty. He may be here at any moment.

deductions.observation: a wire from Hilton Cubitt this morning
deductions.conclusion: there have been some new incidents of importance

deductions.observation: The new dancing men message ('NEVER') was on a different panel of the door, not merely an addition to the first message.
deductions.conclusion: This fact is 'far the most important of all for our purpose' and 'fills me with hopes', indicating it is a crucial clue that advances the investigation.

deductions.observation: A long inscription, 'ELSIE-PREPARE-TO-MEET-THY-GOD', appeared on the pedestal of the sundial at Hilton Cubitt's residence.
deductions.inference: The situation has escalated significantly, indicating an immediate and grave danger to Hilton Cubitt.
deductions.conclusion: Holmes and Watson must travel to North Walsham without delay, as their presence is urgently needed.

deductions.observation: Holmes receives a cablegram.
deductions.inference: The content of the cablegram confirms Holmes's expectations regarding the critical nature and danger of the case.
deductions.conclusion: It is even more essential to inform Hilton Cubitt of the true state of affairs, as he is entangled in a dangerous web.

deductions.observation: Holmes asks, 'Has he been moved?' (referring to Mr. Hilton Cubitt).
deductions.inference: The original position of the body is critical evidence for understanding the crime scene.

deductions.observation: The response, 'We have moved nothing except the lady.'
deductions.inference: Mr. Hilton Cubitt's body is in its original position, but Mrs. Hilton Cubitt's body has been moved for medical attention.
deductions.conclusion: The scene has been partially disturbed, but key evidence regarding Mr. Cubitt's position remains intact.

deductions.observation: Holmes asks, 'How long have you been here, Doctor?'
deductions.inference: The duration of the doctor's presence could indicate the timeline of events or the extent of potential scene disturbance.

deductions.observation: Holmes asks, 'Anyone else?' (present at the scene).
deductions.inference: Identifying all individuals who have been at the crime scene is crucial for gathering witness accounts and assessing potential contamination.

deductions.observation: Holmes asks, 'And you have touched nothing?' (to the Doctor).
deductions.inference: Ascertaining if any evidence has been disturbed by the doctor or others is vital for preserving the integrity of the crime scene.

deductions.observation: The Doctor replies, 'Nothing.' (to 'touched nothing?'), and his overall responses to Holmes's questions.
deductions.inference: The doctor claims to have only moved the lady and touched nothing else, indicating carefulness in his actions at the scene.
deductions.conclusion: You have acted with great discretion.

deductions.observation: There was no powder-marking either upon his dressing-gown or on his hands.
deductions.inference: The absence of the latter means nothing, though its presence may mean everything.

deductions.observation: a hole which had been drilled right through the lower window-sash, about an inch above the bottom.
deductions.inference: A bullet has so obviously struck the edge of the window.
deductions.conclusion: A third shot has been fired, and therefore a third person must have been present.

deductions.observation: the servants said that on leaving their room they were at once conscious of a smell of powder
deductions.inference: It suggested that at the time of the firing, the window as well as the door of the room had been open. Otherwise the fumes of powder could not have been blown so rapidly through the house. A draught in the room was necessary for that.

deductions.observation: the candle was not guttered
deductions.inference: Both door and window were only open for a very short time, however.

deductions.observation: Feeling sure that the window had been open at the time of the tragedy
deductions.inference: I conceived that there might have been a third person in the affair, who stood outside this opening and fired through it.

deductions.observation: I looked, and there, sure enough, was the bullet mark!
deductions.conclusion: There was a third person in the affair, who stood outside this opening and fired through it, and a shot directed at this person hit the sash.

deductions.observation: the window to be shut and fastened
deductions.inference: The woman's first instinct would be to shut and fasten the window.

deductions.observation: splintering of the wood
deductions.inference: this third bullet... has clearly... been fired from inside the room.

deductions.observation: Mrs. King was awakened by a 'loud explosion' and found it 'very loud', but couldn't definitively compare its loudness to the second shot.
deductions.conclusion: it was undoubtedly so (two shots fired almost at the same instant).

deductions.observation: The flowers were trampled down, and the soft soil was imprinted all over with footmarks. Large, masculine feet they were, with peculiarly long, sharp toes.
deductions.inference: Someone with large, masculine feet and peculiarly long, sharp toes was in the garden near the study window.

deductions.observation: Holmes found 'a little brazen cylinder' in the garden.
deductions.inference: the revolver had an ejector, and here is the third cartridge.

deductions.observation: the revolver had an ejector, and here is the third cartridge.
deductions.inference: The discovery of a third cartridge, combined with the revolver's ejector mechanism, provides crucial physical evidence regarding the events of the shooting.
deductions.conclusion: our case is almost complete.

deductions.observation: Holmes observes the 'singular productions' (the dancing men papers) in front of him.
deductions.inference: He infers that this cipher system is 'entirely new to me', despite his extensive familiarity with 'all forms of secret writings' and having authored 'a trifling monograph upon the subject, in which I analyze one hundred and sixty separate ciphers'.

deductions.observation: Holmes observes the nature of the dancing men characters.
deductions.conclusion: He concludes that 'The object of those who invented the system has apparently been to conceal that these characters convey a message, and to give the idea that they are the mere random sketches of children.'

deductions.observation: the symbols stood for letters
deductions.inference: applied the rules which guide us in all forms of secret writings
deductions.conclusion: the solution was easy enough

deductions.observation: Out of fifteen symbols in the first message, four were the same
deductions.inference: E is the most common letter in the English alphabet, and it predominates to so marked an extent that even in a short sentence one would expect to find it most often
deductions.conclusion: the symbol XXX stood for E

deductions.observation: in some cases the figure was bearing a flag, and in some cases not
deductions.inference: it was probable, from the way in which the flags were distributed, that they were used to break the sentence up into words
deductions.conclusion: I accepted this as a hypothesis

deductions.observation: In a single word of five letters, two 'E's appear in the second and fourth positions.
deductions.inference: The word could be 'sever,' 'lever,' or 'never.'
deductions.conclusion: The word is most probably 'never' as a reply to an appeal, and it was likely written by the lady.

deductions.observation: The word 'never' is correct.
deductions.conclusion: The symbols stand for N, V, and R.

deductions.observation: Appeals came from someone who had been intimate with the lady in her early life.
deductions.inference: A combination of symbols containing two 'E's with three letters between might stand for the name 'ELSIE.'

deductions.observation: The combination 'E_ _ _E' formed the termination of a message which was repeated three times.
deductions.conclusion: The message was an appeal to 'Elsie,' and the letters L, S, and I were identified.

deductions.observation: The word preceding 'Elsie' had only four letters and ended in 'E'.
deductions.inference: The word must be 'COME.'

deductions.observation: Other four-letter words ending in 'E' were tried but did not fit the case.
deductions.conclusion: The letters C, O, and M were identified.

deductions.observation: A word in the coded message ended in E.
deductions.inference: Considering common English words, the word must be 'COME.'
deductions.conclusion: The letters C, O, and M were identified.

deductions.observation: The pattern '.M .ERE ..E SL.NE.' was derived from the first message.
deductions.inference: The first letter could only be A, which occurs three times, and H is apparent in the second word.
deductions.conclusion: The message was decoded to 'AM HERE A.E SLANE'.

deductions.observation: The partial name 'A.E SLANE' was identified.
deductions.inference: Filling in obvious vacancies.
deductions.conclusion: The name was 'ABE SLANEY'.

deductions.observation: The second message pattern was 'A. ELRI. ES.'
deductions.inference: Only by putting T and G for the missing letters did it make sense, suggesting a house or inn name.
deductions.conclusion: The second message decoded to 'A. ELRIGES'.

deductions.observation: The name 'Abe' is an American contraction, and a letter from America started the trouble.
deductions.inference: These facts point to an American origin.
deductions.conclusion: Abe Slaney was an American.

deductions.observation: The lady's allusions to her past and her refusal to confide in her husband.
deductions.inference: These behaviors suggest hidden information.
deductions.conclusion: There was some criminal secret in the matter.

deductions.observation: The lady's allusions to her past, and her refusal to take her husband into her confidence
deductions.inference: both pointed in that direction [criminal secret in the matter]
deductions.conclusion: There is a criminal secret in the lady's past.

deductions.observation: The message 'ELSIE .RE.ARE TO MEET THY GO.' with the addition of a P and a D
deductions.inference: showed me that the rascal was proceeding from persuasion to threats
deductions.conclusion: Abe Slaney is escalating his actions from persuasion to threats.

deductions.observation: To fly would be a confession of guilt.
deductions.inference: Abe Slaney is guilty of the crime.
deductions.conclusion: He will not try to escape.

deductions.observation: I have written and asked him.
deductions.inference: Abe Slaney will come because he was asked.
deductions.conclusion: I expect him here every instant.

deductions.observation: here is the gentleman himself coming up the drive.
deductions.inference: The letter I framed has successfully lured the intended recipient.
deductions.conclusion: The person arriving is the suspect I intended to capture.

deductions.observation: The unnamed man's character and past actions towards Elsie (Mrs. Hilton Cubitt).
deductions.inference: Elsie broke away from his influence, fled from America to avoid him, married an honourable gentleman in England, and the unnamed man dogged and followed her.
deductions.conclusion: The unnamed man made Elsie's life a misery to induce her to abandon her husband.

deductions.observation: Abe Slaney asks 'who was it that wrote this note?'
deductions.inference: Holmes needed to lure Slaney to him.
deductions.conclusion: Holmes wrote the note to bring Slaney here.

deductions.observation: Abe Slaney states 'There was no one on earth outside the Joint who knew the secret of the dancing men' and questions how Holmes wrote the note.
deductions.inference: Holmes wrote the note using the dancing men code.
deductions.conclusion: Holmes knew the secret of the dancing men.

deductions.observation: Abe Slaney questions how Holmes knew the secret of the dancing men.
deductions.inference: Holmes possesses superior deductive and investigative skills.
deductions.conclusion: What one man can invent another can discover.

deductions.observation: Holmes's presence and knowledge in the investigation.
deductions.inference: This presence and knowledge saved Mrs. Hilton Cubitt from being formally accused.
deductions.conclusion: Mrs. Hilton Cubitt had herself lain under grave suspicion of the murder of her husband.

deductions.observation: The little line of dancing men: COME-HERE-AT-ONCE
deductions.inference: Using the explained code, the message means 'Come here at once.'
deductions.conclusion: The invitation would not be refused by the recipient, as he would believe it came from the lady.

scenes.title: Holmes's Deduction of Watson's Thoughts
scenes.description: Holmes is engrossed in a chemical experiment when he suddenly reveals his knowledge of Watson's private thoughts about investing in South African securities, astonishing Watson.

scenes.title: Holmes Explains a Deduction to Watson
scenes.description: Holmes explains to Watson how he deduced that Watson had decided against investing in gold fields, detailing the chain of reasoning from a chalk mark to Thurston's property option.

scenes.title: Mr. Hilton Cubitt's Arrival and Presentation of the Dancing Men
scenes.description: Holmes, Inspector Martin, and Mrs. King discuss the bullet trajectory and the sound of the shots in the study. | Holmes, Inspector Martin, the country doctor, the narrator, and a village policeman gather in the old hall. Housemaid Saunders and cook Mrs. King recount being awakened by two explosions, finding Mr. Hilton Cubitt dead and Mrs. Hilton Cubitt severely wounded in the study, noting a burning candle and a shut, fastened window. | Holmes, Martin, and the narrator await the arrival of a suspect. The suspect, a tall, swarthy man, approaches the house. Upon entering, Holmes swiftly subdues him with a pistol, and Martin handcuffs him. The captured man expresses surprise, realizing he has been lured into a trap. | Holmes, after being slightly nettled by Watson's reaction, presents a new, unexplained problem to Watson: a sheet of paper with 'absurd hieroglyphics' sent by Mr. Hilton Cubitt, who is on his way to consult Holmes. | Mr. Abe Slaney recounts the events leading up to and including the shooting of Elsie's husband, his attempt to pull Elsie through a window, and his subsequent escape. | Mr. Hilton Cubitt arrives at Baker Street, meets Holmes and Watson, and immediately shows them the mysterious paper with dancing figures, expressing his concern for his wife. | Sherlock Holmes explains his deductions regarding the open window and the presence of a third person during the shooting to Inspector Martin, confirming his theory with a bullet mark on the sash. He then discovers a lady's handbag containing a large sum of money. | The passage and room are full of smoke and the smell of powder. Servants describe finding the injured couple, moving Mrs. Cubitt, and the state of the study. The window was shut and fastened from the inside, and servants confirm no one could have escaped. Holmes and Inspector Martin prepare to examine the room, where Mr. Hilton Cubitt's body lies, shot from the front through the heart, indicating instantaneous death.

scenes.title: Mr. Hilton Cubitt Recounts His Marriage
scenes.description: After dispatching the boy, Holmes gives instructions to the servants regarding Mrs. Hilton Cubitt's condition and visitors, then leads the way into the drawing-room. | Hilton Cubitt presents the fresh drawing of the new dancing men message ('NEVER') to Holmes, who recognizes its significant importance. | Holmes expresses satisfaction with his findings, writes a telegram, and informs Watson of his expectation to travel to Norfolk. | Holmes recounts his initial steps in deciphering the dancing men code, explaining how he identified the letter 'E' and the purpose of the flags, and the subsequent difficulty that led him to wait for more messages. | Mr. Hilton Cubitt begins to narrate the story of his marriage to Elsie Patrick, providing background to the mysterious dancing men.

scenes.title: Client's concern for Elsie and family honor
scenes.description: The client expresses his deep concern for Elsie's constant fear and defends her character, emphasizing his high regard for family honor.

scenes.title: First appearance of dancing figures
scenes.description: The client recounts finding chalk dancing figures on window-sills about a week ago, initially dismissing them, but Elsie reacted with unexpected seriousness.

scenes.title: Second appearance and Elsie's faint
scenes.description: A week after the first incident, a paper with dancing figures is found on the sundial; Elsie faints upon seeing it and remains in a dazed, terrified state.

scenes.title: Client seeks Holmes's help
scenes.description: The client explains his decision to contact Mr. Holmes, stating that the police would not take him seriously, and expresses his determination to protect Elsie.

scenes.title: Holmes's Discussion with Inspector Martin
scenes.description: Hilton Cubitt expresses his fears for his wife Elsie and presents the hieroglyphics to Holmes. Holmes advises him to speak with Elsie, but Cubitt refuses to break her confidence. Holmes then analyzes the hieroglyphics and concludes more information is needed, advising Cubitt to return to Norfolk. | Holmes explains to a surprised Inspector Martin that he anticipated the crime and came to prevent it, mentioning the 'dancing men' evidence and offering his assistance in the investigation.

scenes.title: Holmes advises Hilton Cubitt
scenes.description: Holmes tells Mr. Hilton Cubitt to return to Norfolk and gather more evidence due to insufficient information for an investigation.

scenes.title: Holmes ponders the dancing men
scenes.description: Over several days, Holmes is seen thoughtfully examining the curious dancing men figures he copied onto a slip of paper.

scenes.title: Hilton Cubitt's urgent wire
scenes.description: A fortnight later, Holmes receives a telegram from Hilton Cubitt indicating new important incidents and his imminent arrival, prompting Holmes to ask Watson to stay.

scenes.title: Hilton Cubitt arrives worried
scenes.description: Hilton Cubitt arrives at Holmes's residence directly from the station, looking worried and depressed, stating the business is getting on his nerves.

scenes.title: Hilton Cubitt's Frustration and Holmes's Advice
scenes.description: After Hilton Cubitt leaves, Holmes meticulously calculates and deciphers the dancing men code for two hours. | Hilton Cubitt expresses his anger and fear regarding the dancing men and his wife's behavior, asking Holmes for advice. Holmes advises against violent remedies and asks Cubitt to leave the papers for his investigation. | Holmes informs Inspector Martin that the case is nearly complete after finding a third cartridge. He then questions the servants about an inn called 'Elrige's', which leads to the stable-boy identifying 'Elrige's Farm' near East Ruston. Holmes decides to send a note to this farm. | Holmes waits impatiently for news, then receives a letter from Hilton Cubitt detailing a new, ominous inscription on a sundial, prompting Holmes's anxiety and decision to act. | Inspector Martin arrives with policemen, arrests Slaney, and expresses gratitude to Mr. Sherlock Holmes as Slaney is taken away in a cab. | The client arrives, visibly distressed, and reports to Mr. Holmes about the worsening situation with the dancing men, his wife's suffering, and presents new dancing men pictures, including having seen the man who draws them.

scenes.title: Client presents new evidence
scenes.description: The client shows Holmes copies of new hieroglyphic messages that have appeared, describing the circumstances of their discovery.

scenes.title: Hilton's vigil and sighting
scenes.description: Hilton waits in his study with a revolver to catch the perpetrator, has an interaction with his wife, and then sees something moving in the shadow of the tool-house.

scenes.title: Confrontation at the Tool-house
scenes.description: Hilton Cubitt observes a dark figure near the tool-house, attempts to confront it, is held back by his wife, and later discovers a new dancing men message on the door.

scenes.title: Waiting for Telegram Response
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson experience a two-day delay and impatience while waiting for an answer to Holmes's telegram.

scenes.title: Letter from Hilton Cubitt
scenes.description: On the evening of the second day, a letter arrives from Hilton Cubitt reporting a new inscription.

scenes.title: Holmes Explains Decoding to Inspector Martin
scenes.description: Holmes meticulously explains his process of decoding the dancing men messages to Inspector Martin and the narrator, revealing the identities of 'Abe Slaney' and 'A. ELRIGES', and his subsequent actions. | Holmes, after realizing the urgency of the situation and receiving a confirming cablegram, decides to take the first train in the morning to North Walsham. | Holmes, deeply despondent and silent, travels by carriage for seven miles towards Riding Thorpe Manor, reflecting on his worst fears.

scenes.title: Arrival at North Walsham
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson arrive at North Walsham, where they are immediately met by the station-master upon mentioning their destination.

scenes.title: Arrival at Riding Thorpe Manor and Meeting Inspector Martin
scenes.description: Holmes and Watson arrive at North Walsham, where the station-master informs them of the shooting of Mr. Hilton Cubitt and his wife at Riding Thorpe Manor. | Upon arriving at Riding Thorpe Manor, Holmes and his companion observe the grounds and are greeted by Inspector Martin of the Norfolk Constabulary.

scenes.title: Journey through East Anglia
scenes.description: Holmes and his companion drive through a singular countryside in East Anglia, observing the landscape and approaching the Norfolk coast.

scenes.title: Crime Scene Examination and Discovery of Third Shot
scenes.description: Holmes, the country doctor, and Inspector Martin examine the bodies of Mr. Cubitt and his wife. Holmes observes the lack of powder-marking on Mr. Cubitt and later points out a bullet hole in the window-sash, leading to the conclusion that a third shot was fired and a third person was involved. | The narrative provides an update on the legal outcome for Abe Slaney and the recovery and future life of Mrs. Hilton Cubitt.

scenes.title: Holmes Explains the Dancing Men
scenes.description: Holmes and Inspector Martin move to the garden to look for evidence, finding footmarks and a cartridge. | In the drawing-room, Holmes prepares to explain the background of the dancing men cipher to Watson and the Inspector, referencing his previous consultations with Mr. Hilton Cubitt.

scenes.title: Holmes Prepares and Dispatches a Note
scenes.description: Holmes works with the dancing men slips, prepares a note for Mr. Abe Slaney at Elriges Farm, and dispatches a boy with it, giving strict instructions. He also advises Inspector Martin to telegraph for an escort.

scenes.title: Holmes recounts his investigation steps
scenes.description: Holmes explains his initial investigation, including cabling Wilson Hargreave for information on Abe Slaney, receiving Slaney's threatening message, and his subsequent journey to Norfolk.

scenes.title: Holmes and Inspector discuss Slaney's capture
scenes.description: Holmes reassures the inspector about Abe Slaney's capture, explaining that Slaney will not attempt to escape and is expected to arrive at their location, having been summoned by Holmes.

scenes.title: Confrontation with the unnamed man
scenes.description: Holmes confronts the unnamed man, who reveals his past relationship with Mrs. Hilton Cubitt and his role in the shooting, while Mrs. Hilton Cubitt is gravely injured.

scenes.title: Holmes confronts Abe Slaney and reveals his knowledge
scenes.description: Holmes sternly confronts Abe Slaney, accusing him of causing the death of Mr. Hilton Cubitt and driving Mrs. Hilton Cubitt to suicide. Slaney questions Holmes about a note written in the dancing men code, which Holmes admits to writing to lure him. Holmes explains his ability to decipher the code and reveals that Mrs. Hilton Cubitt was under suspicion for her husband's murder, urging Slaney to clear her name.

scenes.title: Holmes explains the deciphered note and plans return
scenes.description: Holmes explains the meaning of the dancing men note to Watson, reflecting on its use for good, and they prepare to take a train back to Baker Street.

events.name: Holmes's Deduction on Watson's Investment
events.description: Holmes reveals his deduction about Watson's decision not to invest in gold fields, based on a series of observations and inferences about Watson's habits and acquaintances.

events.name: Instructions Regarding Mrs. Hilton Cubitt
events.description: A dark, creeping figure is seen by Hilton Cubitt in the shadow of the tool-house. | A letter from Hilton Cubitt reaches Holmes, providing an update on the situation. | A long inscription, likely another dancing men message, appears on a pedestal at Hilton Cubitt's location. | A sheet of paper with strange hieroglyphics arrives by post, signaling the beginning of a new case for Holmes, brought by Mr. Hilton Cubitt. | A stable-boy provides information about 'Elrige's Farm', a lonely farm located near East Ruston, where a farmer named Elrige lives. | Elsie's husband rushes in with a revolver during Slaney's attempt to abduct Elsie. | Hilton Cubitt discovers a new arrangement of dancing men, spelling 'NEVER', scrawled on a different panel of the door. | Holmes and Martin swiftly apprehend the arriving suspect, with Holmes using a pistol and Martin applying handcuffs. | Holmes and his companion meet Inspector Martin of the Norfolk Constabulary upon their arrival. | Holmes cables Wilson Hargreave of the New York Police Bureau for information regarding Abe Slaney. | Holmes dispatches a long telegram, expecting a crucial answer related to his findings. | Holmes finds a lady's hand-bag containing twenty fifty-pound notes on the study table, which he deems important for the trial. | Holmes instructs the servants not to reveal Mrs. Hilton Cubitt's condition to visitors and to show any callers into the drawing-room. | Holmes makes his first breakthrough in deciphering the dancing men code, identifying the letter 'E' and hypothesizing the function of flags. | Inspector Martin arrives and arrests Slaney. | Sherlock Holmes successfully deciphers the intricate code of the dancing men through elaborate calculation. | Slaney catches Elsie's arm and tries to pull her through the window. | Slaney flees across the garden after shooting the husband. | Slaney shoots the husband after the husband fires and misses him. | The client arrives to report new findings to Mr. Holmes, including fresh dancing men pictures and having seen the man who draws them. | The man Holmes was expecting arrives at the house, having been lured by a letter. | Through decoding and logical deduction, Holmes identifies Abe Slaney as an American involved in the case. | Upon hearing the tragic news, Holmes becomes utterly despondent, realizing his worst fears have come true.

events.name: Mr. Hilton Cubitt's arrival
events.description: Mr. Hilton Cubitt arrives at Holmes's residence in Baker Street to consult him about the mysterious dancing men.

events.name: Presentation of the dancing men message
events.description: Mr. Hilton Cubitt presents the paper with the curious markings to Holmes, initiating the investigation into the mystery.

events.name: Mr. Hilton Cubitt meets Elsie Patrick
events.description: Mr. Hilton Cubitt meets Elsie Patrick at a boarding-house in Russell Square, London, during the Jubilee.

events.name: Marriage of Mr. Hilton Cubitt and Elsie Patrick
events.description: Mr. Hilton Cubitt and Elsie Patrick quietly marry at a registry office in London and return to Norfolk.

events.name: Elsie's pre-marital confession
events.description: Elsie reveals to Hilton Cubitt that she has a painful past she wishes to keep secret before their marriage.

events.name: Hilton Cubitt's acceptance of Elsie's terms
events.description: Hilton Cubitt agrees to marry Elsie, accepting her condition of silence regarding her past.

events.name: Elsie receives a letter from America
events.description: Elsie receives a letter with an American stamp, which causes her to turn deadly white and burn it.

events.name: Elsie burns the letter
events.description: After reading the distressing letter from America, Elsie immediately throws it into the fire.

events.name: Elsie's persistent fear
events.description: Elsie consistently displays a look of fear and apprehension, as if waiting for something. | Following the receipt and burning of the letter, Elsie lives in a constant state of fear and apprehension.

events.name: Discovery of chalk dancing figures
events.description: The client found absurd little dancing figures scrawled with chalk on one of the window-sills.

events.name: Elsie's serious reaction to figures
events.description: Elsie took the appearance of the dancing figures very seriously and requested to see any future occurrences.

events.name: Discovery of paper with dancing figures
events.description: A paper with dancing figures was found lying on the sundial in the garden.

events.name: Elsie's fainting spell
events.description: Elsie dropped in a dead faint after being shown the paper with dancing figures.

events.name: Client contacts Mr. Holmes
events.description: The client wrote and sent the paper with dancing figures to Mr. Holmes, seeking his assistance.

events.name: Hilton Cubitt seeks Holmes's help
events.description: Hilton Cubitt explains his concern for his wife Elsie and the mysterious hieroglyphics, asking Holmes for assistance.

events.name: Holmes advises Hilton Cubitt to speak with Elsie
events.description: Holmes suggests that Hilton Cubitt directly ask his wife, Elsie, to share her secret with him.

events.name: Hilton Cubitt refuses to force Elsie's confidence
events.description: Hilton Cubitt states he will not compel Elsie to reveal her secret due to a promise, but will pursue his own line of inquiry.

events.name: Holmes agrees to help Hilton Cubitt
events.description: Holmes pledges his full support to Hilton Cubitt in his investigation.

events.name: Holmes questions Hilton Cubitt about strangers
events.description: Holmes inquires if any unfamiliar individuals have been observed in Hilton Cubitt's quiet neighborhood.

events.name: Holmes analyzes the hieroglyphics
events.description: Holmes examines the provided sample of hieroglyphics, noting their potential meaning but concluding that the sample is too short and the facts too indefinite for immediate investigation.

events.name: Holmes advises Hilton Cubitt to return to Norfolk
events.description: Holmes suggests that Hilton Cubitt return to Norfolk to gather more information.

events.name: Holmes advises Hilton Cubitt
events.description: Holmes advises Hilton Cubitt to return to Norfolk, keep a lookout, and collect exact copies of any new dancing men figures.

events.name: Hilton Cubitt sends a wire
events.description: Hilton Cubitt sends a telegram to Holmes, informing him of new incidents and his travel plans to London.

events.name: Holmes and Watson arrive at North Walsham
events.description: Hilton Cubitt arrives at Holmes's residence, visibly distressed by the ongoing mystery of the dancing men. | Upon their arrival at North Walsham, Holmes and Watson are immediately approached by the station-master.

events.name: Discovery of New Dancing Men on Tool-House
events.description: The client found a fresh crop of dancing men drawn in chalk upon the black wooden door of the tool-house.

events.name: Client Sees the Man Who Draws Dancing Men
events.description: The client saw the man responsible for drawing the dancing men pictures.

events.name: Appearance of AT-ELRIGES
events.description: A fresh hieroglyphic inscription 'COME-ELSIE' appears two mornings after the first. | A hieroglyphic message 'AT-ELRIGES' appears, which the client copies.

events.name: Message on the sundial
events.description: A message with characters identical to the last one is found scrawled on paper under a pebble on the sundial.

events.name: Hilton's wife intervenes
events.description: Hilton's wife finds him waiting in his study and tries to persuade him to come to bed, dismissing the messages as a practical joke.

events.name: Sighting near the tool-house
events.description: Hilton sees something dark moving in the shadow of the tool-house while he is on vigil.

events.name: Hilton Cubitt Shows New Message to Holmes
events.description: Elsie brings money to try and bribe Slaney to leave her in peace. | Hilton Cubitt presents the fresh drawing of the new dancing men message to Holmes for examination. | Holmes prepares a note addressed to Mr. Abe Slaney at Elriges Farm and sends a boy to deliver it with strict instructions.

events.name: Hilton Cubitt asks for Holmes's advice
events.description: Hilton Cubitt recounts his frustration with the situation and asks Holmes for a solution.

events.name: Holmes requests the papers
events.description: Holmes asks Hilton Cubitt to leave the papers containing the dancing men messages for his investigation.

events.name: Hilton Cubitt departs
events.description: Hilton Cubitt leaves Holmes's residence to return home.

events.name: Delay in Telegram Response
events.description: The anticipated answer to Holmes's telegram is delayed for two days, causing impatience.

events.name: Appearance of new inscription on sundial
events.description: Hilton Cubitt reports that a threatening inscription, 'ELSIE-PREPARE-TO-MEET-THY-GOD', has appeared on his sundial.

events.name: Holmes decides to travel to North Walsham
events.description: Reacting to the escalating threat, Holmes decides to take the earliest train to North Walsham to intervene personally.

events.name: Holmes receives a confirming cablegram
events.description: A cablegram arrives, which Holmes states confirms his expectations and further emphasizes the urgency of the situation.

events.name: News of the Shooting at Riding Thorpe Manor
events.description: Holmes and Watson learn from the station-master that Mr. Hilton Cubitt has been shot dead and his wife has shot herself, her life hanging by a thread.

events.name: Arrival at Riding Thorpe Manor
events.description: Holmes and his companion arrive at Riding Thorpe Manor after a journey through the countryside.

events.name: Holmes reveals prior knowledge of the crime
events.description: Holmes informs Inspector Martin that he anticipated the crime and came in the hope of preventing it.

events.name: Holmes mentions the dancing men evidence
events.description: Holmes tells Inspector Martin that he possesses the evidence of the dancing men.

events.name: Discovery of Mrs. Hilton Cubitt's wounds
events.description: Mrs. Hilton Cubitt was found badly wounded and is near death. | Saunders and Mrs. King found Mrs. Hilton Cubitt crouching near the window, horribly wounded and incapable of speaking. | The local surgeon reports that Mrs. Hilton Cubitt's injuries are serious but not necessarily fatal, with a bullet having passed through her brain.

events.name: Confirmation of Mr. Hilton Cubitt's death
events.description: It is confirmed that Mr. Hilton Cubitt had been shot through the heart. | Mr. Hilton Cubitt was found dead. | Saunders and Mrs. King descended the stairs and found Mr. Hilton Cubitt lying dead in the center of the study.

events.name: Holmes's initial questioning at the crime scene
events.description: Holmes begins his investigation by questioning the doctor and constable about the state of the bodies and any disturbances to the scene.

events.name: Explosions heard by house staff
events.description: Saunders and Mrs. King were aroused from their sleep by the sound of an explosion, followed by a second one a minute later.

events.name: Servants discover the injured couple
events.description: Servants find Mr. and Mrs. Hilton Cubitt injured after hearing a shot, with the room full of smoke and the smell of powder.

events.name: Initial examination of the study
events.description: Holmes and Inspector Martin prepare to examine the study, where Mr. Hilton Cubitt's body lies, shot through the heart.

events.name: Discovery of the third bullet hole
events.description: Holmes points out a bullet hole in the lower window-sash, indicating that a third shot was fired during the incident.

events.name: Realization of a third person's presence
events.description: Based on the discovery of the third bullet hole, it is concluded that a third person must have been present during the shooting.

events.name: Discovery of the fifty-pound notes
events.description: Twenty fifty-pound notes are found in a bag, which Holmes states must be preserved for trial.

events.name: Discussion of the third bullet
events.description: Holmes discusses the trajectory and origin of the third bullet, noting it was fired from inside the room.

events.name: Mrs. King's testimony on the shots
events.description: Mrs. King is questioned by Holmes about the loudness and sequence of the shots she heard.

events.name: Discovery of footmarks in the garden
events.description: Large, masculine footmarks with long, sharp toes are found in the flower-bed outside the study window.

events.name: Discovery of the third cartridge
events.description: Holmes discovers a third cartridge, which he believes completes the evidence related to the revolver, indicating significant progress in the case. | Holmes finds a little brazen cylinder in the garden, identifying it as the third cartridge from a revolver with an ejector.

events.name: Search for Elrige's
events.description: Holmes questions the servants about an inn or place named 'Elrige's' as part of his investigation.

events.name: Holmes decides to send a note to Elrige's Farm
events.description: After learning about Elrige's Farm, Holmes decides to send a note there, indicating a new lead in the investigation.

events.name: Advice to Telegraph for Escort
events.description: Holmes advises Inspector Martin to telegraph for an escort, anticipating a dangerous prisoner.

events.name: Holmes explains previous consultations
events.description: Holmes begins to recount the circumstances of Mr. Hilton Cubitt's prior visits to Baker Street regarding the dancing men.

events.name: Waiting for Fresh Material
events.description: Holmes decides to wait for more messages due to the difficulty of further deciphering the code with limited material.

events.name: Second interview with Mr. Hilton Cubitt
events.description: Mr. Hilton Cubitt provided Holmes with two short sentences and one message composed of dancing men symbols.

events.name: Decoding of the Dancing Men messages
events.description: Holmes successfully deciphers the coded messages, identifying 'Abe Slaney' and 'A. ELRIGES'.

events.name: Holmes cables Wilson Hargreave
events.description: Holmes cables his friend Wilson Hargreave of the New York Police Bureau to inquire about Abe Slaney.

events.name: Hilton Cubitt sends Slaney's last message
events.description: Hilton Cubitt sends Holmes the final message from Abe Slaney, which contains threats.

events.name: Holmes deciphers Slaney's message
events.description: Holmes deciphers the coded message from Abe Slaney, realizing it signifies an escalation from persuasion to threats.

events.name: Holmes travels to Norfolk
events.description: Holmes and Dr. Watson travel to Norfolk, arriving after the tragic events have already occurred.

events.name: Holmes expects Abe Slaney's arrival
events.description: Holmes reveals he has written to Abe Slaney and expects him to arrive at their current location at any moment.

events.name: Unnamed man's arrival
events.description: The unnamed man arrived at the current location in response to a letter from Mrs. Hilton Cubitt.

events.name: Unnamed man's confession of shooting
events.description: The unnamed man admits to shooting Mr. Hilton Cubitt, claiming self-defense or justification.

events.name: Elsie's flight and marriage
events.description: Mrs. Hilton Cubitt (Elsie) fled from America to escape the unnamed man and married Hilton Cubitt in England.

events.name: Unnamed man's pursuit of Elsie
events.description: The unnamed man relentlessly pursued Mrs. Hilton Cubitt (Elsie) after her marriage, making her life miserable.

events.name: Holmes confronts Abe Slaney
events.description: Holmes sternly accuses Abe Slaney of his past actions and responsibility for the tragic events involving the Cubitts.

events.name: Holmes reveals he wrote the dancing men note
events.description: Abe Slaney questions who wrote the note in the dancing men code, and Holmes admits he wrote it to bring Slaney to him.

events.name: Holmes reveals Mrs. Hilton Cubitt's suspicion
events.description: Holmes informs Abe Slaney that Mrs. Hilton Cubitt was suspected of her husband's murder and that his intervention saved her.

events.name: Abe Slaney agrees to confess
events.description: Abe Slaney agrees to tell the 'absolute naked truth' to clear Mrs. Hilton Cubitt's name.

events.name: Patrick invents the dancing men writing
events.description: Elsie's father, Patrick, invents a secret writing system that looks like a child's scrawl.

events.name: Elsie leaves the Chicago gang
events.description: Elsie, having some honest money, gives the gang the slip and moves to London.

events.name: Slaney comes to England
events.description: After Elsie's marriage, Slaney travels to England to find her and send her messages.

events.name: Elsie writes an answer to Slaney's messages
events.description: Elsie responds to one of Slaney's messages, indicating she reads them.

events.name: Slaney's Departure with Police
events.description: Slaney is taken away in a cab by Inspector Martin and uniformed policemen.

events.name: Abe Slaney's condemnation and sentence change
events.description: Abe Slaney was condemned to death at the winter assizes at Norwich, but his penalty was changed to penal servitude due to mitigating circumstances and the certainty that Hilton Cubitt had fired the first shot.

events.name: Mrs. Hilton Cubitt's recovery and new life
events.description: Mrs. Hilton Cubitt recovered entirely from her injuries, remains a widow, and devotes her life to the care of the poor and the administration of her husband's estate.
